title: Three Children Killed in Bushfire in Kwilu’s Bagata Territory
excerpt: Bagata, Kwilu, July 13, 2026 - Three children have died after becoming trapped in a bushfire in Luie village, Bagata Territory, in Kwilu Province, prompting local authorities to ban bush burning during the dry season. According to local officials, four children had gone into…
title_en: Three Children Killed in Bushfire in Kwilu’s Bagata Territory
excerpt_en: Bagata, Kwilu, July 13, 2026 - Three children have died after becoming trapped in a bushfire in Luie village, Bagata Territory, in Kwilu Province, prompting local authorities to ban bush burning during the dry season. According to local officials, four children had gone into…
body_en:
Bagata, Kwilu, July 13, 2026 - Three children have died after becoming trapped in a bushfire in Luie village, Bagata Territory, in Kwilu Province, prompting local authorities to ban bush burning during the dry season.
According to local officials, four children had gone into a nearby forest to collect ginger when they were caught in a fire allegedly started by unidentified adults who fled the area after igniting the vegetation.
Two of the children died at the scene, while a third later succumbed to severe burns at Ndanu Hospital. A fourth child survived and alerted the village to the incident.
Local authorities said the two children who died at the scene were from the same family. They reportedly attempted to escape the flames by climbing a small tree, but were unable to avoid the rapidly spreading fire. The victims were between 11 and 13 years old.
Following the tragedy, Manzasay Sector Chief Nuclette Tankuyi announced an immediate ban on bush burning during the dry season, warning that the practice poses a serious threat to nearby communities.
The incident has renewed concerns about the dangers of uncontrolled bushfires in rural areas, where seasonal burning is often used to clear land for agricultural activities. During the dry season, such fires can spread rapidly, endangering lives, homes, and farmland.
The latest tragedy follows similar incidents in Kwilu Province. In July 2024, a bushfire destroyed 25 houses in Nkara village in Bulungu Territory, highlighting the recurring risks associated with uncontrolled vegetation burning during the dry season.

title: Wazalendo Fighters Retake Strategic Town of Katoy in North Kivu
excerpt: Masisi, North Kivu, July 13, 2026 - Wazalendo fighters have regained control of the strategic town of Katoy in Masisi Territory, North Kivu, following intense clashes with AFC/M23 rebels, marking another shift in the volatile security landscape of eastern Democratic Republic…
title_en: Wazalendo Fighters Retake Strategic Town of Katoy in North Kivu
excerpt_en: Masisi, North Kivu, July 13, 2026 - Wazalendo fighters have regained control of the strategic town of Katoy in Masisi Territory, North Kivu, following intense clashes with AFC/M23 rebels, marking another shift in the volatile security landscape of eastern Democratic Republic…
body_en:
Masisi, North Kivu, July 13, 2026 - Wazalendo fighters have regained control of the strategic town of Katoy in Masisi Territory, North Kivu, following intense clashes with AFC/M23 rebels, marking another shift in the volatile security landscape of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The fighting reportedly began on July 12 when Wazalendo forces launched an offensive from the Waloa Loanda area in neighboring Walikale Territory. Heavy and light weapons fire echoed across Katoy for several hours as both sides battled for control of the town.
The violence triggered panic among residents of Katoy and nearby villages, forcing many civilians to flee their homes in search of safer areas amid fears of escalating hostilities.
According to local reports, the Wazalendo ultimately succeeded in dislodging AFC/M23 fighters from the town. The rebels reportedly withdrew toward the Ngungu axis, while Wazalendo forces moved to reinforce their newly established positions and secure control of the area.
No official information has been released regarding casualties or material losses, and independent verification remains difficult because of the persistent insecurity affecting the region.
The recapture of Katoy comes amid renewed fighting between Wazalendo groups and AFC/M23 across the territories of Masisi and Walikale. The recurring clashes have continued to displace civilians, disrupt economic activity, and deepen the humanitarian crisis across North Kivu, underscoring the fragile security situation that persists in eastern DRC.

title: Nansana Leaders Warn Health Workers Over Alleged Patient Extortion
excerpt: Nansana, Uganda, July 13, 2026 - Leaders in Nansana Division have vowed to take action against health workers accused of demanding illegal payments from patients, particularly pregnant women seeking services at government health facilities. Speaking during a division council…
title_en: Nansana Leaders Warn Health Workers Over Alleged Patient Extortion
excerpt_en: Nansana, Uganda, July 13, 2026 - Leaders in Nansana Division have vowed to take action against health workers accused of demanding illegal payments from patients, particularly pregnant women seeking services at government health facilities. Speaking during a division council…
body_en:
Nansana, Uganda, July 13, 2026 - Leaders in Nansana Division have vowed to take action against health workers accused of demanding illegal payments from patients, particularly pregnant women seeking services at government health facilities.
Speaking during a division council meeting, Nansana Division Chairperson Sam Mugabi condemned the alleged practice, describing it as unlawful and a violation of public trust. He warned that health workers found demanding money from patients would face disciplinary measures and possible arrest.
Mugabi said residents should be able to access public healthcare services without being subjected to unofficial charges, adding that the division leadership would work with relevant authorities to address corruption within government health facilities.
The warning comes amid concerns over reports of patients being asked to pay for services that are supposed to be provided free of charge in public facilities.
During the same meeting, the division’s internal security officials urged councillors to focus on protecting residents and avoid shielding individuals involved in criminal activities. Leaders were encouraged to put aside political differences and work together to improve community safety and service delivery.
The newly constituted Nansana Division Council also pledged to strengthen accountability, promote unity among leaders, and improve public services for residents.

title: Sama Lukonde Presents DRC as a “Solution Country” on Climate Change and Condemns Environmental Impact of Eastern Conflict
excerpt: Yaoundé, July 13, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo used the 51st Session of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Francophonie (APF) in Cameroon to highlight its environmental potential and call for stronger international support in addressing the consequences of…
title_en: Sama Lukonde Presents DRC as a “Solution Country” on Climate Change and Condemns Environmental Impact of Eastern Conflict
excerpt_en: Yaoundé, July 13, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo used the 51st Session of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Francophonie (APF) in Cameroon to highlight its environmental potential and call for stronger international support in addressing the consequences of…
body_en:
Yaoundé, July 13, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo used the 51st Session of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Francophonie (APF) in Cameroon to highlight its environmental potential and call for stronger international support in addressing the consequences of insecurity in the east of the country.
Held from July 6 to 11 in Yaoundé, the Francophone parliamentary gathering brought together more than 300 lawmakers representing 42 parliamentary sections from across the Francophone world. The DRC’s delegation was led by Senate President Jean-Michel Sama Lukonde Kyenge, who placed climate change and the security crisis in eastern Congo at the center of his intervention.
Speaking during the session, Sama Lukonde emphasized the strategic role of the DRC in global environmental protection, presenting the country as a major contributor to climate solutions due to its vast forests, biodiversity, and natural resources.
“Our country naturally positions itself as a true solution-oriented country,” he said, highlighting the importance of the Congo Basin, the world’s second-largest tropical rainforest, and its critical role in regulating the global climate.
The Senate President also highlighted the Kivu-Kinshasa Green Corridor initiative, a vast conservation and development project covering more than 500,000 square kilometers aimed at supporting climate action, protecting ecosystems, and promoting sustainable development.
However, he warned that decades of crises have weakened the country’s ability to fully contribute to global environmental efforts. According to him, international responses remain insufficient considering the scale of both ecological challenges and the pressures facing communities dependent on forest resources.
Sama Lukonde also linked armed conflicts to environmental destruction, accusing the ongoing instability in eastern DRC involving the AFC/M23 movement of causing severe humanitarian and ecological damage. He argued that violence has resulted not only in deaths and displacement but also in the destruction of ecosystems, wildlife, vegetation, and water resources.
“We cannot claim to ensure climate balance as long as we plunder and massively destroy natural resources through war,” he warned, calling for stronger international engagement in support of peace initiatives and the implementation of existing agreements aimed at ending the conflict.
The Senate President urged Francophone countries to support a genuine climate partnership based on solidarity, particularly by taking into account the needs of communities living near forest areas. He also announced Kinshasa’s support for Juliana Lumumba’s candidacy for the leadership of the International Organisation of La Francophonie.
Beyond high-level discussions, the APF session provided a platform for Francophone parliamentarians to debate political, democratic, economic, social, cultural, and environmental challenges affecting member countries.
The event also included the 11th edition of the Francophone Youth Parliament, which brought together 61 young participants from 29 French-speaking parliamentary sections, alongside representatives from partner institutions. The initiative, supported by Francophone organizations for more than two decades, aims to strengthen youth participation in democratic dialogue and international cooperation.
Through its participation in Yaoundé, the DRC sought to reinforce its diplomatic message: positioning itself not only as a country rich in natural resources, but also as a key actor in global climate solutions while calling for greater attention to the environmental consequences of conflicts affecting its territory.

title: President Guelleh Offers Condolences Following the Death of Qatar’s Former Emir
excerpt: Djibouti City, July 13, 2026 - President Ismail Omar Guelleh has extended his heartfelt condolences to the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim Bin Hamad Al-Thani, following the passing of his father and former Emir, Sheikh Hamad Bin Khalifa Al-Thani. In a message of condolence…
title_en: President Guelleh Offers Condolences Following the Death of Qatar’s Former Emir
excerpt_en: Djibouti City, July 13, 2026 - President Ismail Omar Guelleh has extended his heartfelt condolences to the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim Bin Hamad Al-Thani, following the passing of his father and former Emir, Sheikh Hamad Bin Khalifa Al-Thani. In a message of condolence…
body_en:
Djibouti City, July 13, 2026 - President Ismail Omar Guelleh has extended his heartfelt condolences to the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim Bin Hamad Al-Thani, following the passing of his father and former Emir, Sheikh Hamad Bin Khalifa Al-Thani.
In a message of condolence addressed to the Qatari leader, President Guelleh expressed his deep sympathy and solidarity with the Emir, the Qatari people, and the ruling family during this period of mourning.
The Djiboutian head of state paid tribute to the late Sheikh Hamad Bin Khalifa Al-Thani, describing him as a visionary leader whose reforms laid the foundations for Qatar's modern development, economic prosperity, and growing international influence.
President Guelleh also highlighted the late former Emir's contribution to strengthening the close relationship between Djibouti and Qatar, noting that bilateral ties experienced significant growth during Sheikh Hamad's leadership and established the basis for the enduring partnership between the two countries.
Conveying condolences on behalf of the people and government of Djibouti, President Guelleh offered prayers for the late leader and expressed hope that his legacy of leadership and service would continue to inspire future generations.
The message reaffirmed Djibouti's solidarity with the State of Qatar as it mourns the loss of one of the country's most influential modern leaders.
Economy and Tech.

title: Kinshasa Pushes Natural Resources Governance to the Center of Global Peace Debate
excerpt: Kinshasa, July 13, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo is seeking to place the governance of natural resources at the heart of international discussions on peace and security during its presidency of the United Nations Security Council. For Kinshasa, the management of…
title_en: Kinshasa Pushes Natural Resources Governance to the Center of Global Peace Debate
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, July 13, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo is seeking to place the governance of natural resources at the heart of international discussions on peace and security during its presidency of the United Nations Security Council. For Kinshasa, the management of…
body_en:
Kinshasa, July 13, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo is seeking to place the governance of natural resources at the heart of international discussions on peace and security during its presidency of the United Nations Security Council. For Kinshasa, the management of strategic resources is no longer only an economic issue but a major factor influencing conflicts, stability, and global security.
After opening its Security Council presidency agenda with a high-level debate on conflict-related sexual violence on July 8, the DRC is now turning attention to the relationship between natural resources and peace through an “Arria-formula” meeting scheduled for July 13. The diplomatic initiative will reach a higher level on July 22, when President Félix Tshisekedi is expected to chair a ministerial-level debate on “the governance of natural resources as a foundation for peace, security, and prosperity.”
A Call for a New International Framework
Through this initiative, Kinshasa aims to encourage a broader international debate on what it describes as a gap in global approaches to natural resources and conflict prevention.
While mechanisms such as mineral traceability systems, corporate responsibility standards, and measures against conflict financing already exist, the Congolese authorities argue that these efforts remain fragmented and lack a unified strategy.
The objective is therefore to promote a more integrated international framework connecting responsible resource management, conflict prevention, and long-term security.
For the DRC, natural resources should no longer be considered solely through the lens of trade, investment, or economic development. They should also be treated as a strategic security issue requiring greater attention from the United Nations Security Council.
Critical Minerals and Rising Global Stakes
The initiative comes amid growing global demand for critical minerals essential to batteries, digital technologies, and the energy transition. Countries rich in strategic resources are increasingly becoming central to global economic competition, while concerns over illegal exploitation and resource-driven conflicts continue to attract international attention.
Kinshasa argues that greater transparency, improved traceability, shared responsibility among stakeholders, and a fairer distribution of resource benefits could contribute to preventing instability and reducing the risk of conflicts linked to natural wealth.
A Broader Diplomatic Strategy
Since taking over the presidency of the Security Council, the DRC has focused on themes that extend beyond its own national challenges.
The July 8 debate on conflict-related sexual violence highlighted issues such as survivor protection, accountability, prevention, and strengthening international responses. With the natural resources debate, Kinshasa is expanding its diplomatic agenda toward another structural issue: the connection between resource governance, armed conflicts, and international peace.
Seeking Long-Term Influence at the Security Council
The choice of the “Arria-formula” format for the July 13 meeting allows broader participation from regional organizations, experts, civil society representatives, and private sector actors alongside Security Council members.
Rather than seeking immediate decisions, the DRC’s strategy focuses on shaping the international conversation and building support for a stronger global approach to natural resource governance.
Through these diplomatic initiatives, Kinshasa hopes to establish natural resources as a permanent element of the Security Council’s discussions, alongside traditional security concerns such as armed conflicts, sanctions, and civilian protection.

title: Four Dead and More Than 50 Inmates Escape During Prison Break in Bulungu
excerpt: Bulungu, July 13, 2026 - At least four people were killed and more than 50 inmates escaped from the central prison of Bulungu, in Kwilu province, following an attempted mass breakout on Sunday evening. The incident occurred when prisoners reportedly forced open the main…
title_en: Four Dead and More Than 50 Inmates Escape During Prison Break in Bulungu
excerpt_en: Bulungu, July 13, 2026 - At least four people were killed and more than 50 inmates escaped from the central prison of Bulungu, in Kwilu province, following an attempted mass breakout on Sunday evening. The incident occurred when prisoners reportedly forced open the main…
body_en:
Bulungu, July 13, 2026 - At least four people were killed and more than 50 inmates escaped from the central prison of Bulungu, in Kwilu province, following an attempted mass breakout on Sunday evening.
The incident occurred when prisoners reportedly forced open the main entrance of the facility around 8:00 p.m. Security forces fired warning shots in an attempt to stop the escape, resulting in the deaths of three inmates and one police officer, according to local sources.
Out of the 63 detainees who escaped, only a small number have so far been recaptured. Local civil society reported that five inmates were initially found and arrested, while prison officials later indicated that only three had been recovered.
The escaped detainees included 58 men, five women, and one infant. According to local authorities, only eight of the escapees had already been convicted, while the majority were awaiting trial after spending several months in detention.
The police officer suspected of using his weapon during the incident has reportedly been arrested and is facing legal proceedings.

KAMPALA, July 13, 2026 - Twelve Ugandan creative entrepreneurs have completed a year-long business incubation programme designed to transform cultural and creative ventures into commercially sustainable enterprises.
The entrepreneurs, working in areas including fashion, product design, crafts, agriculture and cultural innovation, graduated after receiving business training, mentorship, market support and seed funding to expand their ventures.
The incubation programme focused on strengthening Uganda’s creative economy by helping entrepreneurs improve business planning, financial management, branding, market access and long-term growth strategies.
Participants highlighted challenges commonly faced by creative businesses, including limited access to finance, professional networks and opportunities to reach wider markets.
Organisers said the creative sector should be recognised as an important contributor to economic growth, employment creation and cultural identity, rather than being viewed only as an artistic field.
Among the graduates were entrepreneurs developing innovative businesses in specialised areas such as sericulture and design, who said the programme helped them establish clearer strategies, improve operations and prepare for future expansion.
The initiative also emphasised the importance of promoting locally made products and strengthening the global visibility of Ugandan creative enterprises.
Graduates received seed funding to support business expansion, while stakeholders called for continued investment in the creative industries as a growing source of jobs and economic opportunities.

excerpt: Masisi, July 13, 2026 - Heavy fighting broke out early Sunday morning in the Bashali Mokoto area of Masisi territory, North Kivu, after an attack attributed to AFC/M23 forces against positions held jointly by the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and…
title_en: FARDC and VDP Report Repelling AFC/M23 Assault Near Nkingwe as Civilians Flee Fighting
excerpt_en: Masisi, July 13, 2026 - Heavy fighting broke out early Sunday morning in the Bashali Mokoto area of Masisi territory, North Kivu, after an attack attributed to AFC/M23 forces against positions held jointly by the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and…
body_en:
Masisi, July 13, 2026 - Heavy fighting broke out early Sunday morning in the Bashali Mokoto area of Masisi territory, North Kivu, after an attack attributed to AFC/M23 forces against positions held jointly by the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and the Volunteers for the Defense of the Homeland (VDP).
The clashes began around 6:00 a.m. near Nkingwe, a strategic position located close to the village of Malemo. According to local and security sources, AFC/M23 fighters launched an offensive aimed at taking control of the area.
After several hours of exchanges of fire, FARDC and VDP forces said they had resisted the attack and forced the rebels to withdraw from some positions. Local sources reported that two AFC/M23 defensive positions were abandoned during the fighting.
The provisional assessment provided by local security actors mentions the recovery of military equipment, including a PKM machine gun and four AK-47 rifles. Two individuals suspected of belonging to AFC/M23 were also reportedly captured and transferred to Pinga.
The clashes triggered renewed population movements in the area. Residents of Nkingwe and Malemo, fearing further violence, fled their homes and sought refuge in Kalembe.
Despite the reported withdrawal of AFC/M23 elements from certain positions, the security situation remains fragile. Local sources indicate that Malemo is still divided, with some areas under the control of FARDC and VDP forces while others remain influenced by AFC/M23 fighters.
The situation continues to raise fears of renewed confrontations in this part of Masisi territory, where repeated clashes between armed groups and government forces have intensified insecurity among civilian communities.

title: DRC Doctors’ Strike Continues as SYNAMED Rejects Government Claims of Agreement
excerpt: Kinshasa, July 13, 2026 - The doctors’ strike in public hospitals affiliated with the National Union of Doctors (SYNAMED) is continuing despite government statements announcing the end of the movement following a reported agreement with medical unions. SYNAMED’s provincial…
title_en: DRC Doctors’ Strike Continues as SYNAMED Rejects Government Claims of Agreement
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, July 13, 2026 - The doctors’ strike in public hospitals affiliated with the National Union of Doctors (SYNAMED) is continuing despite government statements announcing the end of the movement following a reported agreement with medical unions. SYNAMED’s provincial…
body_en:
Kinshasa, July 13, 2026 - The doctors’ strike in public hospitals affiliated with the National Union of Doctors (SYNAMED) is continuing despite government statements announcing the end of the movement following a reported agreement with medical unions.
SYNAMED’s provincial executive secretary for Kinshasa, Dr. Patrick Boloko, rejected the government’s announcement, arguing that the conclusions presented after the 94th meeting of the Council of Ministers do not reflect the position of doctors on the ground.
According to the union representative, the minutes of discussions between doctors and government officials were rejected by the rank and file, who considered that the document contained no clear commitments or guarantees regarding their demands.
Dr. Boloko explained that a working session was held with the Minister of Health, resulting in the signing of meeting minutes. However, he criticized the fact that the document did not include concrete financial commitments from key government officials responsible for budgetary decisions, particularly the Deputy Prime Minister in charge of the Budget and the Minister of Finance.
For SYNAMED, ending the strike cannot be decided solely by union representatives but must be approved by doctors themselves. Since the rank and file rejected the report, the union maintains that the strike remains active.
The doctors are demanding several measures, including the integration of additional payments into the third-quarter payroll process, the inclusion of at least 800 doctors on the official salary scale, and the regularization of thousands of medical professionals who currently work without salaries or benefits.
The union also criticized delays in implementing salary adjustments, arguing that quarterly reviews expected in January and April were not carried out, increasing frustration among medical staff.
The dispute escalated after SYNAMED launched its “Hospitals Without Doctors” operation on July 7, following weeks of unsuccessful negotiations with authorities. The movement was initially announced from July 7 to 16, 2026, across the country, except in Ituri, North Kivu, and South Kivu provinces.
During the strike, only emergency services and blood banks were expected to remain operational, with urgent cases redirected to designated healthcare facilities.
SYNAMED maintains that dialogue remains possible and says it is willing to continue negotiations with the government. However, the union insists that concrete commitments must be made before doctors consider suspending their action.
The disagreement highlights growing tensions between medical professionals and authorities over working conditions, salary adjustments, and the implementation of previously discussed commitments within the public health sector.

title: DRC Calls for Stronger Defense of State Sovereignty at Francophone Parliamentary Assembly
excerpt: Yaoundé, Cameroon, July 13, 2026 - The Speaker of the National Assembly of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Aimé Boji Sangara, used the 51st Session of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Francophonie (APF) to call for stronger international action in defense of state…
title_en: DRC Calls for Stronger Defense of State Sovereignty at Francophone Parliamentary Assembly
excerpt_en: Yaoundé, Cameroon, July 13, 2026 - The Speaker of the National Assembly of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Aimé Boji Sangara, used the 51st Session of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Francophonie (APF) to call for stronger international action in defense of state…
body_en:
Yaoundé, Cameroon, July 13, 2026 - The Speaker of the National Assembly of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Aimé Boji Sangara, used the 51st Session of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Francophonie (APF) to call for stronger international action in defense of state sovereignty, respect for international law, and multilateralism, while condemning what he described as Rwanda's aggression in eastern DRC.
Addressing Francophone parliamentarians during the gathering held in Yaoundé from July 6 to 11, Boji argued that respect for territorial integrity and the inviolability of internationally recognized borders remain fundamental principles of the United Nations Charter and the international order.
He warned that violations of these principles undermine the credibility of multilateral institutions and weaken the global rules-based system designed to preserve peace and security.
Focusing on the security situation in eastern DRC, the Speaker accused Rwanda of supporting the AFC/M23 rebellion and blamed the conflict for one of the region's most severe humanitarian crises. He highlighted the widespread displacement of civilians, the loss of lives, and the continued suffering of vulnerable populations, particularly women and children.
Boji called on the international community to move beyond statements of concern and adopt a more consistent approach in enforcing international commitments. He argued that multilateralism cannot remain credible if violations of state sovereignty and international agreements continue without accountability.
He also urged respect for United Nations Security Council resolutions calling for the protection of the DRC's sovereignty, an end to support for armed groups, and the withdrawal of foreign forces operating on Congolese territory.
Reaffirming the principles of the Francophonie, Boji emphasized that the organization is built on shared values of peace, the rule of law, solidarity, and respect for human dignity. He said multilateral institutions should remain committed to defending justice and protecting the sovereignty of member states rather than remaining silent in the face of aggression.
At the same time, the Speaker reaffirmed the Democratic Republic of Congo's commitment to maintaining peaceful relations with neighboring countries under the leadership of President Félix Tshisekedi, stressing that Kinshasa continues to support regional cooperation and good neighborliness.
The 51st Session of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Francophonie brought together more than 300 parliamentarians from 42 parliamentary sections. Throughout the week, delegates discussed a broad range of political, democratic, economic, social, cultural, and environmental issues affecting the Francophone community, highlighting the role of parliamentary diplomacy in addressing shared international challenges.

title: Tshisekedi Orders End to Illegal Military Presence at Mining Sites to Strengthen Resource Governance
excerpt: Kinshasa, July 13, 2026 — President Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi has ordered the immediate withdrawal of all military personnel and members of the Congolese National Police (PNC) illegally present at mining sites across the Democratic Republic of Congo, as part of efforts to…
title_en: Tshisekedi Orders End to Illegal Military Presence at Mining Sites to Strengthen Resource Governance
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, July 13, 2026 — President Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi has ordered the immediate withdrawal of all military personnel and members of the Congolese National Police (PNC) illegally present at mining sites across the Democratic Republic of Congo, as part of efforts to…
body_en:
Kinshasa, July 13, 2026 — President Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi has ordered the immediate withdrawal of all military personnel and members of the Congolese National Police (PNC) illegally present at mining sites across the Democratic Republic of Congo, as part of efforts to improve transparency, security, and governance in the strategic mining sector.
Speaking during the 94th meeting of the Council of Ministers held on July 10, 2026, at the African Union City in Kinshasa, the Head of State reaffirmed the importance of mining resources for the country’s economic development while stressing the need to restore confidence among investors and international partners.
The DRC, which holds some of the world’s largest reserves of critical minerals essential for global energy transition technologies, has placed mining-sector reform at the center of its economic strategy. However, authorities continue to face challenges linked to illegal exploitation, weak oversight mechanisms, and interference by security forces in mining operations.
President Tshisekedi warned that the unauthorized presence of armed personnel at mining sites damages the country’s reputation, weakens state control, and encourages illegal activities that undermine responsible resource management.
According to the government, the involvement of uniformed personnel in mining areas contributes to intimidation, harassment, extortion, disruption of mineral traceability systems, and the development of smuggling networks.
The President stressed that security forces may only intervene in mining areas when their presence is legally authorized or officially requested by competent authorities. He rejected any occupation or interference that could compromise the rights of legitimate mining operators and local communities.
To enforce this decision, Félix Tshisekedi instructed several senior officials, including the Deputy Prime Minister in charge of Interior and Security, the Deputy Prime Minister responsible for Defense, the Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), and the Commissioner General of the Congolese National Police, to immediately implement measures aimed at eliminating illegal militarization of mining zones.
The measures include the removal of unauthorized military and police personnel from mining sites, the prevention of security-force interference in mining activities, the protection of legally established operations, and the dismantling of fraud and illegal mining networks benefiting from protection by uniformed individuals.
The Head of State also called for exemplary sanctions against those involved in illegal occupation of mining sites and urged the strengthening of mechanisms for mineral certification, traceability, and supply-chain monitoring.
The government’s renewed action comes amid longstanding concerns over the role of security forces in mining areas. For several years, civil society organizations and authorities have reported cases of abuse, illegal taxation, intimidation, and unauthorized exploitation of mineral resources.
Similar measures had already been announced in 2022, when the government ordered the withdrawal of military and police personnel from artisanal mining sites following reports of irregularities.
Through this new directive, Kinshasa aims to reinforce state authority over natural resources, improve the credibility of the mining sector, and align the country’s mineral governance with international standards at a time when global demand for strategic minerals continues to grow.

title: Sudan Reaffirms Support for Peace Mediation While Reviewing Proposal
excerpt: KHARTOUM, July 13, 2026 - Sudan’s Security and Defence Council has reaffirmed its commitment to peace efforts, announcing that it is engaging positively with a mediation proposal presented by international facilitators while maintaining conditions aimed at safeguarding the…
title_en: Sudan Reaffirms Support for Peace Mediation While Reviewing Proposal
excerpt_en: KHARTOUM, July 13, 2026 - Sudan’s Security and Defence Council has reaffirmed its commitment to peace efforts, announcing that it is engaging positively with a mediation proposal presented by international facilitators while maintaining conditions aimed at safeguarding the…
body_en:
KHARTOUM, July 13, 2026 - Sudan’s Security and Defence Council has reaffirmed its commitment to peace efforts, announcing that it is engaging positively with a mediation proposal presented by international facilitators while maintaining conditions aimed at safeguarding the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The council, chaired by Sovereign Council Chairman and Armed Forces Commander-in-Chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, reviewed the proposed framework during a regular meeting and agreed on a unified government response.
Officials said Sudan remains open to initiatives that reflect the aspirations of the Sudanese people and preserve the country's unity, independence, and territorial integrity.
The council also dismissed reports circulating on social media regarding the contents of the negotiations, urging restraint in publishing information that could affect national security or undermine ongoing peace efforts.
The latest discussions follow the presentation of an international peace proposal outlining a roadmap for ending the conflict, which recently prompted diplomatic consultations between Sudanese officials and international mediators.
While expressing support for mediation, Sudanese authorities reiterated that any future agreement must be acceptable to both the government and the Sudanese people. Officials also stressed that military operations would continue alongside diplomatic efforts.
The peace initiative has generated mixed reactions among Sudan’s political groups, with some viewing it as an opportunity to advance negotiations, while others argue that it does not adequately address the conditions necessary to end the conflict.
The government has consistently maintained that any formal negotiations require the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) to withdraw from territories under their control and assemble their fighters in designated locations before a broader political settlement can move forward.
Economy and Tech.

title: Sudan Court Sentences RSF Leader Hemetti to Death in Absentia Over Darfur Atrocities
excerpt: PORT SUDAN, July 12, 2026 — A Sudanese counter-terrorism court has sentenced Rapid Support Forces (RSF) commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemetti, to death in absentia, alongside two of his brothers and 13 other defendants, over crimes committed during the…
title_en: Sudan Court Sentences RSF Leader Hemetti to Death in Absentia Over Darfur Atrocities
excerpt_en: PORT SUDAN, July 12, 2026 — A Sudanese counter-terrorism court has sentenced Rapid Support Forces (RSF) commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemetti, to death in absentia, alongside two of his brothers and 13 other defendants, over crimes committed during the…
body_en:
PORT SUDAN, July 12, 2026 — A Sudanese counter-terrorism court has sentenced Rapid Support Forces (RSF) commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemetti, to death in absentia, alongside two of his brothers and 13 other defendants, over crimes committed during the conflict in West Darfur.
The court found the defendants guilty of charges including war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide linked to the violence in El Geneina, the capital of West Darfur State.
Among the cases cited was the 2023 killing of West Darfur Governor Khamis Abakar, who was detained before being killed during intense fighting in the city.
In addition to Hemetti, the court sentenced his brothers Abdelrahim Dagalo and Al-Qoni Hamdan Dagalo, as well as several senior RSF commanders, local leaders, and individuals accused of participating in the attacks.
The court ruled that the convicted individuals were responsible for widespread attacks on civilians, destruction and looting of property, forced displacement, and assaults on residential neighbourhoods, schools, and places of worship.
Authorities also ordered the confiscation of RSF assets in favour of the Sudanese government and directed state institutions to seek international arrest notices through Interpol for the convicted individuals.
The court stated that the crimes fall under international law and are not subject to statutes of limitation or political pardons.
The violence in West Darfur during 2023 resulted in large-scale civilian casualties and forced tens of thousands of members of the Masalit community to flee across the border into eastern Chad, creating one of the conflict’s largest displacement crises.

title: U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham, Known for Views on AFC/M23 and Great Lakes Security, Dies at 71
excerpt: WASHINGTON, July 12, 2026 - U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham, a prominent Republican figure known for his influence on foreign policy and national security issues, has died at the age of 71, his office announced. Graham’s office said he died Saturday night following a “brief and…
title_en: U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham, Known for Views on AFC/M23 and Great Lakes Security, Dies at 71
excerpt_en: WASHINGTON, July 12, 2026 - U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham, a prominent Republican figure known for his influence on foreign policy and national security issues, has died at the age of 71, his office announced. Graham’s office said he died Saturday night following a “brief and…
body_en:
WASHINGTON, July 12, 2026 - U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham, a prominent Republican figure known for his influence on foreign policy and national security issues, has died at the age of 71, his office announced.
Graham’s office said he died Saturday night following a “brief and unexpected illness.” His family requested prayers and support as they mourn his death.
First elected to the U.S. Senate in 2003, Graham became one of the most influential Republican voices on foreign affairs, defense policy, and international security. He served as chairman of the Senate Budget Committee and was preparing to seek another six-year Senate term in November.
Emergency services were reportedly called to his Capitol Hill residence late Saturday after reports of a possible heart attack. Images from the scene showed emergency responders transporting a person from the residence to an ambulance.
Graham’s death came shortly after a visit to Kyiv, Ukraine, where he met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He had also been scheduled to appear on NBC’s “Meet the Press” program.
Graham’s Position on Eastern DRC Conflict
In the Great Lakes region, Lindsey Graham was known for his views on the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and his public comments regarding the AFC/M23 movement.
In December 2025, he welcomed the AFC/M23 announcement that it would withdraw from Uvira but expressed concern over continued attacks against the group.
He called for renewed diplomatic engagement, saying that the United States should encourage all parties to return to negotiations.
Graham argued that peace talks were essential and aligned with efforts promoted by U.S. President Donald Trump to support peace and economic development in the Great Lakes region.
Previous Engagement in the Great Lakes Region
Graham had previously engaged with issues affecting the Great Lakes region. In 2013, he was among a group of U.S. senators who visited the region and discussed security challenges, including the role of the United Nations peacekeeping mission.
At the time, he said international support was important but emphasized that long-term stability would require a political solution involving countries and communities in the region.
“There has to be a political solution,” he said, calling for greater cooperation among the Democratic Republic of Congo, neighboring countries, and regional actors.
In December 2025, Graham also met with Rwandan President Paul Kagame to discuss strengthening Rwanda-U.S. cooperation in areas including security, environmental protection, and economic development.
Further details regarding the circumstances of his death are expected as authorities continue to provide information.
Economy and Tech.

title: Ukraine Denies Supporting AFC/M23 and Accuses Russia of Spreading Disinformation Over Great Lakes Crisis
excerpt: Kyiv, July 12, 2026 - Ukraine has rejected accusations from Russia alleging that Kyiv supports the AFC/M23 rebellion in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, describing the claims as unfounded and part of what it called a broader disinformation campaign. The reaction came…
title_en: Ukraine Denies Supporting AFC/M23 and Accuses Russia of Spreading Disinformation Over Great Lakes Crisis
excerpt_en: Kyiv, July 12, 2026 - Ukraine has rejected accusations from Russia alleging that Kyiv supports the AFC/M23 rebellion in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, describing the claims as unfounded and part of what it called a broader disinformation campaign. The reaction came…
body_en:
Kyiv, July 12, 2026 - Ukraine has rejected accusations from Russia alleging that Kyiv supports the AFC/M23 rebellion in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, describing the claims as unfounded and part of what it called a broader disinformation campaign.
The reaction came after Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, during a working visit to Bujumbura, Burundi, on Saturday, July 11, accused Ukraine of being among the foreign actors allegedly supporting the armed movement controlling parts of North Kivu and South Kivu provinces.
Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi dismissed the allegations, stating that they were not supported by any evidence and categorically denying any involvement by Kyiv in supporting AFC/M23.
According to the Ukrainian diplomat, his country does not seek to interfere in African conflicts and remains focused on its own security challenges. He instead accused Russia of pursuing destabilizing policies on the African continent.
Heorhii Tykhyi further claimed that Moscow was attempting to attribute to others actions that Ukraine says are linked to Russian activities abroad, including support for armed groups and recruitment of foreign nationals in conflicts.
Kyiv also argued that the accusations were politically motivated and intended to weaken international diplomatic initiatives aimed at resolving the crisis in the Great Lakes region.
The Ukrainian government said Russia’s objective was to undermine United States-led mediation efforts and shift attention away from what it described as Moscow’s own role in international conflicts.
The exchange comes as eastern DRC remains trapped in a prolonged security crisis despite ongoing diplomatic initiatives, including the Washington Agreement and the Doha peace process. Relations between Kinshasa and Kigali remain tense, with both sides offering different interpretations of existing commitments.
The Doha negotiations, supported by Qatar, have also struggled to achieve major breakthroughs, with disagreements persisting between the Congolese government and the AFC/M23 movement, which Kinshasa accuses of being backed by Rwanda.
Regional and international actors continue to call on all parties to respect their commitments and support peace efforts. However, the gap between diplomatic agreements and the realities on the ground remains significant, as fighting continues and each side maintains its own interpretation of the ongoing negotiations.

title: DRC Identifies More Than 63,500 Suspicious Police Records in Workforce Audit
excerpt: Kinshasa, July 12, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has identified more than 63,500 potentially irregular personnel records within the Congolese National Police (PNC), as the government intensifies efforts to strengthen payroll management and improve administrative…
title_en: DRC Identifies More Than 63,500 Suspicious Police Records in Workforce Audit
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, July 12, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has identified more than 63,500 potentially irregular personnel records within the Congolese National Police (PNC), as the government intensifies efforts to strengthen payroll management and improve administrative…
body_en:
Kinshasa, July 12, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has identified more than 63,500 potentially irregular personnel records within the Congolese National Police (PNC), as the government intensifies efforts to strengthen payroll management and improve administrative governance.
During the 94th meeting of the Council of Ministers, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of the Interior, Security, Decentralization and Customary Affairs, Jacquemain Shabani, presented preliminary findings from an ongoing audit of police personnel, revealing significant anomalies in the national police database.
According to the report, authorities reviewed 157,886 personnel records, identifying 63,817 priority cases requiring further investigation. These files include inactive employees, individuals suspected of being fictitious workers, and personnel with irregular administrative status who will undergo physical verification.
The government estimates that failing to address these irregularities could result in financial losses ranging from US$8.32 million to US$19.42 million per month, equivalent to approximately US$99.8 million to US$233 million annually.
Officials say the audit forms part of a broader effort to modernize the management of the Congolese National Police through physical, administrative, and biometric verification of personnel.
To support the initiative, the government plans to mobilize additional resources to finance the nationwide verification exercise and the issuance of biometric identification cards for police officers. Authorities describe the project as a strategic investment aimed at improving workforce management, strengthening administrative oversight, and eliminating irregularities within the police payroll.
The operational phase of the verification program was approved following a high-level evaluation meeting held in Kinshasa on July 9. The meeting brought together senior government officials, representatives of the Congolese National Police, and technical partners to validate the audit's initial findings and prepare for the nationwide deployment of the verification process.
Through the initiative, the government aims to improve transparency in public administration, reduce payroll fraud, and ensure that public resources allocated to the police force are directed to legitimately employed personnel.

title: Report Accuses Sudan’s Warring Parties of Systematic Air Attacks on Civilians in Darfur
excerpt: KAMPALA, July 12, 2026 - A new report has accused both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of repeatedly carrying out air and drone strikes that have deliberately targeted civilians across Darfur, raising serious concerns over violations of…
title_en: Report Accuses Sudan’s Warring Parties of Systematic Air Attacks on Civilians in Darfur
excerpt_en: KAMPALA, July 12, 2026 - A new report has accused both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of repeatedly carrying out air and drone strikes that have deliberately targeted civilians across Darfur, raising serious concerns over violations of…
body_en:
KAMPALA, July 12, 2026 - A new report has accused both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of repeatedly carrying out air and drone strikes that have deliberately targeted civilians across Darfur, raising serious concerns over violations of international humanitarian law.
The report documents 17 air and drone attacks between October 2024 and April 2026, alleging that marketplaces, hospitals, wedding celebrations, mosques, and shelters for displaced people were among the locations hit, resulting in hundreds of civilian deaths and injuries.
According to the findings, investigators identified repeated failures by both sides to distinguish between military objectives and civilian sites during military operations.
Among the incidents highlighted are airstrikes that reportedly struck crowded public areas in Nyala and Tora, as well as a drone attack on a mosque in El Fasher during dawn prayers. The report also alleges the use of so-called "double-tap" strikes, in which a second attack follows shortly after an initial strike, hitting first responders and civilians attempting to rescue victims.
The document describes Sudan’s conflict as increasingly dominated by drones and other advanced aerial weapons, arguing that the growing use of unmanned aircraft has become a major driver of civilian casualties.
The report calls on the international community to strengthen enforcement of existing arms embargoes, curb the flow of weapons into the conflict, and provide greater support for efforts to document violations and monitor arms supply networks.
Researchers behind the report said the continued attacks on civilian infrastructure demonstrate a persistent disregard for the laws of armed conflict and stressed the need for accountability through independent investigations and international justice mechanisms.
Conclusion
The developments between July 1 and 13, 2026 illustrate a conflict that is becoming increasingly entrenched, with military, humanitarian, economic, and diplomatic crises reinforcing one another. The war has evolved beyond conventional frontlines into a struggle for strategic towns, transport corridors, and economic assets, while shifting local alliances and repeated territorial gains and losses continue to fuel instability across Darfur, Kordofan, and the Blue Nile region.
The humanitarian toll continues to deepen. Intensified fighting, drone strikes, and restrictions on humanitarian access have displaced thousands more civilians, overwhelmed cities such as El Obeid, and further strained already fragile health, water, and food systems. Reports of attacks on civilian infrastructure, markets, medical facilities, and displacement sites, alongside mounting allegations of violations of international humanitarian law, have heightened concerns over civilian protection and accountability.
Diplomatic efforts have gained momentum but remain uncertain. Sudan has engaged with international peace initiatives, including a U.S.-backed mediation framework, while reaffirming conditions centered on national sovereignty, territorial integrity, and security arrangements. At the same time, the African Union, the United Nations, and other regional and international partners have intensified efforts to revive negotiations, reflecting growing recognition that a military solution alone is unlikely to end the conflict.
International scrutiny has also increased through legal and political actions, including calls for tougher sanctions, investigations into alleged war crimes, and judicial proceedings against senior figures accused of atrocities. These developments underscore the expanding international dimension of the crisis and the growing emphasis on accountability alongside conflict resolution.
Meanwhile, Sudan's economy remains under severe pressure. Inflation, disrupted trade, declining agricultural production, and damaged infrastructure continue to undermine livelihoods despite government measures to stabilize the currency, support farmers, modernize strategic infrastructure, and strengthen regional economic partnerships.
Taken together, these developments point to a country facing a prolonged and multidimensional crisis. Without sustained progress toward a nationwide ceasefire, expanded humanitarian access, meaningful political dialogue, and economic recovery, Sudan is likely to remain caught in a cycle of violence, displacement, and institutional fragility with consequences extending well beyond its borders.
By Jeff Buleli

title: Salomon Kalonda Warns Against “Constitutional Coups” and Calls for Stronger Electoral Safeguards in Africa
excerpt: Addis Ababa, July 11, 2026 - Congolese Senator Salomon Kalonda Idi Della has called for stronger protections for democratic processes in Africa, warning against what he described as the growing risk of “constitutional coups” during a parliamentary forum on intelligence,…
title_en: Salomon Kalonda Warns Against “Constitutional Coups” and Calls for Stronger Electoral Safeguards in Africa
excerpt_en: Addis Ababa, July 11, 2026 - Congolese Senator Salomon Kalonda Idi Della has called for stronger protections for democratic processes in Africa, warning against what he described as the growing risk of “constitutional coups” during a parliamentary forum on intelligence,…
body_en:
Addis Ababa, July 11, 2026 - Congolese Senator Salomon Kalonda Idi Della has called for stronger protections for democratic processes in Africa, warning against what he described as the growing risk of “constitutional coups” during a parliamentary forum on intelligence, security, and electoral integrity held in Ethiopia.
Speaking before the Ethiopian Parliament, the senator from Haut-Katanga used the situation in the Democratic Republic of Congo as a case study, arguing that ongoing discussions around constitutional reform could potentially open the way for President Félix Tshisekedi to seek a third term, which he considers contrary to constitutional principles.
Addressing the issue of public opposition to the reform initiative, Kalonda denounced what he described as repression against demonstrations organized by opposition groups and civil society. He accused the international community of remaining silent in the face of these developments, saying that such silence risks being interpreted as acceptance rather than neutrality.
The senator drew a distinction between traditional military takeovers and what he called constitutional power grabs, arguing that the latter are more difficult to challenge because they operate through legal mechanisms while potentially undermining democratic principles.
“There are no bad coups on one side and good coups on the other,” Kalonda argued, calling for equal international attention to all forms of unconstitutional changes of power.
Beyond the Congolese context, the senator highlighted broader challenges affecting electoral credibility across Africa. He pointed to concerns over the independence of electoral commissions, the use of judicial institutions to exclude political candidates, and restrictions on internet access during electoral result announcements.
According to Kalonda, these practices weaken public confidence in electoral systems and contribute to political instability on the continent.
To address these challenges, the Congolese senator proposed several measures, including the creation of a permanent African electoral monitoring mechanism, greater investment in digital electoral sovereignty, transparent and inclusive electoral audits, and a parliamentary observation framework covering the entire electoral cycle from voter registration to the announcement of final results.
He also linked democratic governance to economic competition, particularly in the mining sector, arguing that weak institutions and limited accountability can affect the ability of African countries to negotiate fairly with international economic partners.
Through his intervention in Addis Ababa, Kalonda called on African institutions and international actors to strengthen democratic safeguards and ensure that electoral processes remain transparent, credible, and inclusive.

title: DRC Highlights Population Census as Cornerstone of Data-Driven Development on World Population Day
excerpt: Kinshasa, July 11, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has reaffirmed its commitment to evidence-based development planning, with the Second General Population and Housing Census (RGPH-2) positioned as a central pillar of the government's strategy to improve public policy…
title_en: DRC Highlights Population Census as Cornerstone of Data-Driven Development on World Population Day
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, July 11, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has reaffirmed its commitment to evidence-based development planning, with the Second General Population and Housing Census (RGPH-2) positioned as a central pillar of the government's strategy to improve public policy…
body_en:
Kinshasa, July 11, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has reaffirmed its commitment to evidence-based development planning, with the Second General Population and Housing Census (RGPH-2) positioned as a central pillar of the government's strategy to improve public policy and resource allocation.
Marking World Population Day, celebrated annually on July 11, Minister of State for Planning and Coordination of Development Aid, Guylain Nyembo, emphasized the importance of reliable demographic data in shaping policies that respond to the needs of the country's growing population, particularly its youth.
This year's global theme, "Realizing the hopes and aspirations of young people, today and for the future," served as the backdrop for the government's message, which highlighted the role of young people as a driving force for the country's economic and social transformation.
Nyembo described the Congolese population as one of the nation's greatest assets, stressing that the country's demographic strength extends beyond its vast territory and abundant natural resources. He also paid tribute to young people affected by the ongoing conflict in eastern DRC, including displaced persons, students whose education has been disrupted, and victims of violence.
The minister underscored that effective development planning depends on accurate demographic information, describing the RGPH-2 as a strategic tool that will provide a clearer picture of the country's population distribution, social needs, and development priorities.

title: Sudan Relocates War Victims from Makeshift Graves Ahead of Rainy Season
excerpt: KHARTOUM, July 11, 2026 - Sudanese authorities have begun relocating the remains of war victims from temporary burial sites across Khartoum as part of an urgent effort to complete exhumations before the onset of the rainy season. Officials said the remains of 27 victims were…
title_en: Sudan Relocates War Victims from Makeshift Graves Ahead of Rainy Season
excerpt_en: KHARTOUM, July 11, 2026 - Sudanese authorities have begun relocating the remains of war victims from temporary burial sites across Khartoum as part of an urgent effort to complete exhumations before the onset of the rainy season. Officials said the remains of 27 victims were…
body_en:
KHARTOUM, July 11, 2026 - Sudanese authorities have begun relocating the remains of war victims from temporary burial sites across Khartoum as part of an urgent effort to complete exhumations before the onset of the rainy season.
Officials said the remains of 27 victims were transferred from makeshift graves in the Central Market area to official cemeteries in coordination with forensic specialists.
The operation forms part of a wider campaign launched to remove bodies buried in public spaces, residential neighbourhoods, and marketplaces during the height of the conflict, when heavy fighting and the collapse of public services left families with few options for formal burials.
Authorities said all exhumations are being carried out under established legal procedures, including documenting each case, informing relatives where possible, and identifying unknown victims before reburial in designated cemeteries.
The relocation effort is also intended to prepare Khartoum for the return of displaced residents by improving public safety and restoring normal conditions in the capital.
In parallel with the exhumation programme, government authorities are working to rehabilitate essential infrastructure damaged during the conflict, including water, electricity, healthcare, and education services.
Hundreds of mass graves have been discovered across Khartoum since government forces regained control of parts of the capital. Authorities believe many contain victims of enforced disappearances, torture, and other killings that occurred during periods of fighting, and investigations into the sites are continuing.
Justice and Rights

title: Internal Rivalries and Power Struggles Expose Deep Divisions Within AFC/M23
excerpt: Kinshasa, July 11, 2026 - Internal tensions over political ambitions, military strategy, and control of resources are increasingly dividing the Congo River Alliance/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23), according to findings highlighting growing disagreements within the armed group…
title_en: Internal Rivalries and Power Struggles Expose Deep Divisions Within AFC/M23
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, July 11, 2026 - Internal tensions over political ambitions, military strategy, and control of resources are increasingly dividing the Congo River Alliance/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23), according to findings highlighting growing disagreements within the armed group…
body_en:
Kinshasa, July 11, 2026 - Internal tensions over political ambitions, military strategy, and control of resources are increasingly dividing the Congo River Alliance/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23), according to findings highlighting growing disagreements within the armed group operating in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The leadership structure of the AFC/M23 remains marked by a fragile balance between its political and military wings. The movement’s military command continues to be attributed to General Sultani Makenga, although his influence has reportedly faced increasing challenges from within the organization and from external actors. Political leadership remains associated with Bertrand Bisimwa and Corneille Nangaa, the former president of the Independent National Electoral Commission (CENI).
The group’s leaders have continued to benefit from support and guidance from Rwandan authorities and intelligence structures, according to the findings. However, beyond external backing, internal divisions have become more visible, particularly over the movement’s objectives and future direction.
Political ambitions appear to be one of the main sources of disagreement. Figures such as Corneille Nangaa and former Congolese President Joseph Kabila have reportedly expressed ambitions linked to gaining influence over national power in Kinshasa, while several senior M23 commanders have opposed expanding military operations beyond North and South Kivu.
Disputes over the management and distribution of resources have also fueled tensions among senior officials. Some members of the movement have reportedly raised concerns about perceived preferential treatment benefiting certain Tutsi officers and fighters, adding another layer of friction within the organization.
Militarily, the AFC/M23 territories under its control have reportedly been reorganized into three main defense zones. The first zone, covering Nyiragongo, Rutshuru, and Lubero territories, is led by General Baudoin Ngaruye. The second zone, covering Masisi and Walikale, is commanded by Brigadier General Justin Gacheri Musanga, while General Innocent Byamungu oversees operations in South Kivu.
The movement’s armed forces are estimated at around 30,000 fighters. This force reportedly includes former members of the National Congress for the Defence of the People (CNDP), fighters from the original M23 movement, new recruits mobilized since 2021, and individuals coming from diaspora communities and refugee camps in Rwanda.
The ranks have also reportedly expanded through the integration of former members of the Congolese army (FARDC), the Congolese National Police, Wazalendo fighters, local defense groups, and newly established police units, following battlefield developments and the capture of strategic areas in eastern DRC.
These developments come as diplomatic efforts aimed at restoring peace in eastern Congo continue to face major obstacles. Despite the signing of the Washington Agreement and several follow-up discussions, insecurity and humanitarian challenges remain severe, while disagreements between Kinshasa and Kigali continue to complicate implementation of the commitments.
The Doha peace process, facilitated by Qatar, has also struggled to achieve a breakthrough. Several rounds of negotiations between the Congolese government and the AFC/M23 have failed to resolve key disagreements, while additional mediation efforts, including talks held in Switzerland, have yet to produce significant progress.
As diplomatic initiatives slow down and security conditions deteriorate, the future of eastern DRC remains uncertain, with political rivalries, military fragmentation, and competition over strategic resources continuing to shape the conflict landscape.

title: AFC/M23 Has No Formal Alliance with Thomas Lubanga’s CRP/FRP, UN Report Says
excerpt: Kinshasa, July 11, 2026 - The political-military movement led by former Congolese warlord Thomas Lubanga, the Convention for the People’s Revolution/Forces for the People’s Revolution (CRP/FRP), has not established any official cooperation with the AFC/M23 rebellion, despite…
title_en: AFC/M23 Has No Formal Alliance with Thomas Lubanga’s CRP/FRP, UN Report Says
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, July 11, 2026 - The political-military movement led by former Congolese warlord Thomas Lubanga, the Convention for the People’s Revolution/Forces for the People’s Revolution (CRP/FRP), has not established any official cooperation with the AFC/M23 rebellion, despite…
body_en:
Kinshasa, July 11, 2026 - The political-military movement led by former Congolese warlord Thomas Lubanga, the Convention for the People’s Revolution/Forces for the People’s Revolution (CRP/FRP), has not established any official cooperation with the AFC/M23 rebellion, despite publicly expressing support for the movement, according to recent assessments on the security situation in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The CRP/FRP, created on January 10, 2025, continues to promote a political agenda centered on regional autonomy while maintaining an anti-government position, according to the latest analysis of armed groups operating in eastern DRC.
Thomas Lubanga publicly announced his support for AFC/M23 on July 16, 2025, as part of an effort to align his movement with broader regional dynamics and avoid political isolation. However, no formal partnership between the two groups has been reported so far.
The CRP/FRP leadership includes former military figures, political actors, and local personalities from Ituri province, with several members having previously lived in exile in Uganda. The movement is reportedly led militarily by Lobho Gokpa Justin, a former FARDC colonel.
The group has experienced internal difficulties, including leadership defections that weakened its cohesion. Despite these challenges, its ranks reportedly expanded from an estimated 300 fighters in November 2025 to nearly 1,000 members by mid-2026.
The movement has recruited fighters from different communities, including members of the Hema community and former members of the Zaire armed group. Recruitment efforts have also targeted internally displaced persons’ camps in Ituri and refugee camps in Uganda.
Since January 2026, Innocent Kaina, a sanctioned former M23 figure, has reportedly collaborated with the CRP/FRP by helping recruit individuals from refugee communities in Uganda, including former M23 fighters.
Despite these efforts, the movement has struggled to gain broad support among other armed groups and local communities in Ituri. Attempts by CRP/FRP leaders to mobilize young Lendu fighters reportedly produced limited results.
The emergence of the CRP/FRP comes amid continued instability in Ituri, a province affected for years by armed violence, displacement, and inter-community tensions. The movement presents itself as an opposition force against what it describes as failures of state governance and insecurity affecting local populations.
Thomas Lubanga, a former leader of the Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC), was convicted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in 2012 for the war crime of recruiting and using children under the age of 15 in armed conflict. He was sentenced to 14 years in prison and released in 2020 after serving his sentence.
Following his release, Lubanga participated in government-backed peace initiatives in Ituri aimed at encouraging communities to reject armed groups. However, those efforts did not produce the expected results, while his later political activities remained controversial.
The current evolution of the CRP/FRP adds another layer of complexity to the already fragmented security landscape in eastern DRC, where numerous armed movements continue to compete for influence, territory, and political legitimacy.

title: Uganda Airlines Told to Embrace Private Sector Reforms for Growth
excerpt: KAMPALA, July 11, 2026 - Uganda Airlines has been urged to adopt private sector management principles and undertake major reforms aimed at improving efficiency, profitability and competitiveness in the aviation sector. The Ministry of Finance said the national carrier must…
title_en: Uganda Airlines Told to Embrace Private Sector Reforms for Growth
excerpt_en: KAMPALA, July 11, 2026 - Uganda Airlines has been urged to adopt private sector management principles and undertake major reforms aimed at improving efficiency, profitability and competitiveness in the aviation sector. The Ministry of Finance said the national carrier must…
body_en:
KAMPALA, July 11, 2026 - Uganda Airlines has been urged to adopt private sector management principles and undertake major reforms aimed at improving efficiency, profitability and competitiveness in the aviation sector.
The Ministry of Finance said the national carrier must strengthen its commercial approach, improve operational performance and position itself as a reliable international airline capable of supporting Uganda’s broader economic growth ambitions.
The airline’s leadership has been encouraged to focus on sustainable business practices, stronger financial management and improved service delivery to transform the carrier into a world-class aviation company.
Uganda Airlines outlined plans to expand its network through the introduction of new routes, including connections to Accra and Kigali, as part of efforts to strengthen its regional and international presence.
The carrier also introduced a revised flight schedule as it continues efforts to improve operations and respond to changing market conditions.
However, the airline faces several challenges, including disruptions caused by regional conflicts, rising global fuel prices and public health concerns that have affected some operations.
Management has called for a specialised aviation procurement framework to simplify processes related to aircraft acquisition, leasing and purchasing aviation-specific equipment and services.
The airline’s board has also highlighted the need for additional capital investment to support fleet expansion, meet growing passenger demand and improve operational reliability.
Since its relaunch, Uganda Airlines has increased its presence at Entebbe International Airport and continues efforts to strengthen its position as a regional aviation player.

title: Rwanda Defence Forces Honor Retired Soldiers for Years of Service and Sacrifice
excerpt: KIGALI, July 11, 2026 - The Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) have honored retired soldiers and officers who completed their military service, recognizing their loyalty, professionalism, and contribution to the country’s security and development. The recognition ceremony, held on…
title_en: Rwanda Defence Forces Honor Retired Soldiers for Years of Service and Sacrifice
excerpt_en: KIGALI, July 11, 2026 - The Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) have honored retired soldiers and officers who completed their military service, recognizing their loyalty, professionalism, and contribution to the country’s security and development. The recognition ceremony, held on…
body_en:
KIGALI, July 11, 2026 - The Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) have honored retired soldiers and officers who completed their military service, recognizing their loyalty, professionalism, and contribution to the country’s security and development.
The recognition ceremony, held on July 10, 2026, at RDF Headquarters in Kimihurura, Gasabo District, marked the 14th event of its kind dedicated to retired military personnel and those who completed their service contracts.
The ceremony was presided over by Defence Minister Juvenal Marizamunda, who represented President Paul Kagame, the Commander-in-Chief of the RDF. It was attended by RDF Chief of Defence Staff Gen. Mubarakh Muganga, senior military officials, officers, and families of the retired soldiers.
In his remarks, Minister Marizamunda praised the retirees for their commitment to national service, highlighting their role in Rwanda’s liberation struggle, the efforts to stop the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, and the reconstruction of the country.
He also recognized their contribution to building an RDF that is professional, respected internationally, and capable of participating in peacekeeping missions around the world.
According to the minister, the retirees helped establish a legacy of discipline, cooperation, and service that continues to shape the armed forces today.
Minister Marizamunda also acknowledged the support provided by the wives and families of retired soldiers, noting the sacrifices they made while their spouses carried out military duties.
RDF Chief of Defence Staff Gen. Mubarakh Muganga praised the retired personnel for their patriotism, integrity, and professionalism throughout their careers.
He highlighted their role in mentoring and training younger soldiers, passing on RDF values and helping prepare a new generation of military personnel committed to protecting Rwanda’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Gen. Muganga said the RDF and the country will continue to benefit from the experience, knowledge, and advice of retired officers.
Speaking on behalf of the retirees, Maj. Gen. (Rtd) Emmanuel Bayingana expressed pride in the progress achieved by the RDF and thanked President Kagame for his leadership in strengthening the military institution.
He said that although they are leaving active military service, retired officers will continue promoting RDF values, including patriotism, integrity, and dedication to national development.
The ceremony concluded with the awarding of certificates to retired soldiers in recognition of their distinguished service and commitment to the Rwanda Defence Forces.
