title: Jumia Expands E-Commerce Reach Beyond Uganda’s Major Cities
excerpt: KAMPALA, July 10, 2026 - Online shopping is gradually expanding beyond Uganda’s major urban centres as digital platforms invest in logistics networks, local partnerships and technology-driven delivery solutions to reach more communities across the country. For years,…
title_en: Jumia Expands E-Commerce Reach Beyond Uganda’s Major Cities
excerpt_en: KAMPALA, July 10, 2026 - Online shopping is gradually expanding beyond Uganda’s major urban centres as digital platforms invest in logistics networks, local partnerships and technology-driven delivery solutions to reach more communities across the country. For years,…
body_en:
KAMPALA, July 10, 2026 - Online shopping is gradually expanding beyond Uganda’s major urban centres as digital platforms invest in logistics networks, local partnerships and technology-driven delivery solutions to reach more communities across the country.
For years, customers outside Kampala and other large municipalities faced challenges accessing e-commerce services due to long delivery times, high transport costs and limited logistics infrastructure.
The expansion of pick-up stations and improved delivery networks is now helping bridge the gap, allowing customers in districts such as Moroto, Kapchorwa, Arua, Gulu and Kabale to access products through online marketplaces.
The company said the focus is on ensuring customers receive consistent service regardless of their location, with reliability becoming a key priority in areas where road conditions, distance and weather can affect last-mile delivery.
Rather than relying only on home deliveries, the platform has adopted a hybrid logistics model combining urban deliveries with strategically placed collection points in other regions.
The system allows customers to collect parcels from nearby locations, reducing transport costs and improving efficiency in areas where direct delivery may be difficult.
Local entrepreneurs have also become part of the expansion strategy by operating community-based pick-up stations. These partnerships provide easier access points for customers while helping businesses grow alongside the digital commerce sector.
Technology has played a major role in improving operations, with route optimisation systems helping reduce transport costs, improve vehicle utilisation and streamline delivery networks.
The company said operational decisions, including where to establish new collection points, are guided by customer demand and logistics data to improve efficiency.
As e-commerce adoption grows, maintaining customer confidence remains a major focus, with service reliability, successful deliveries and efficient returns systems considered essential to building trust among new online shoppers.
Future plans include exploring electric vehicles for urban deliveries as part of efforts to reduce operational costs and improve environmental sustainability.
With continued investment in logistics, technology and local partnerships, digital commerce is expected to become increasingly accessible to consumers beyond Uganda’s traditional urban markets.

excerpt: Mwenga, July 10, 2026 - AFC/M23 fighters have taken control of Kipupu, a key locality in the Itombwe sector of Mwenga territory, South Kivu, following clashes with armed Wazalendo groups operating in the area. According to local sources, the takeover occurred on Friday, July…
title_en: AFC/M23 Takes Control of Kipupu in Mwenga Territory After Clashes With Wazalendo
excerpt_en: Mwenga, July 10, 2026 - AFC/M23 fighters have taken control of Kipupu, a key locality in the Itombwe sector of Mwenga territory, South Kivu, following clashes with armed Wazalendo groups operating in the area. According to local sources, the takeover occurred on Friday, July…
body_en:
Mwenga, July 10, 2026 - AFC/M23 fighters have taken control of Kipupu, a key locality in the Itombwe sector of Mwenga territory, South Kivu, following clashes with armed Wazalendo groups operating in the area.
According to local sources, the takeover occurred on Friday, July 10, after fighting erupted between AFC/M23 elements and Wazalendo positions. Witnesses reported the use of drones during the operation, alongside exchanges of fire between the opposing forces.
Local authorities and community leaders confirmed the presence in Kipupu of armed elements from Twirwaheno and Red Tabara, groups reported to be allied with AFC/M23.
The renewed fighting has caused further displacement among residents of Kipupu and surrounding villages, according to local civil society representatives. Many inhabitants reportedly fled their homes seeking safer areas as tensions increased.
The capture of Kipupu marks another shift in the security situation in the highlands of South Kivu, a region that has experienced repeated confrontations between armed groups competing for territorial influence.
Kipupu had previously fallen under AFC/M23 control in December 2025 following military operations linked to the group’s advance toward Uvira. The latest developments indicate the continued volatility of the security situation in Mwenga territory and the wider highlands of South Kivu.

title: Displacement Crisis Deepens in El Obeid as Conflict Tightens Grip on City
excerpt: EL OBEID, July 10, 2026 - El Obeid, the capital of Sudan’s North Kordofan State, is facing mounting humanitarian pressure as tens of thousands of displaced people continue to arrive despite an ongoing siege and repeated drone attacks. The city has become a major refuge for…
title_en: Displacement Crisis Deepens in El Obeid as Conflict Tightens Grip on City
excerpt_en: EL OBEID, July 10, 2026 - El Obeid, the capital of Sudan’s North Kordofan State, is facing mounting humanitarian pressure as tens of thousands of displaced people continue to arrive despite an ongoing siege and repeated drone attacks. The city has become a major refuge for…
body_en:
EL OBEID, July 10, 2026 - El Obeid, the capital of Sudan’s North Kordofan State, is facing mounting humanitarian pressure as tens of thousands of displaced people continue to arrive despite an ongoing siege and repeated drone attacks.
The city has become a major refuge for civilians fleeing violence in South and West Kordofan, even as it remains surrounded on three sides by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The deteriorating security situation has heightened concerns over the safety of residents and the possibility of a broader military offensive.
Drone strikes have repeatedly targeted critical infrastructure and the city's main supply route linking El Obeid to Kosti in White Nile State. The attacks have disrupted transport, damaged commercial vehicles, and contributed to sharp increases in the prices of food and other essential goods.
Between March and June, more than 11,000 families, representing around 60,000 people, reportedly arrived in El Obeid, pushing the city's population to an estimated 3.2 million. Nearly half of the residents are now internally displaced, living in temporary camps or with host families.
The growing humanitarian emergency has been compounded by the collapse of local economic activity. Many displaced families struggle to meet their daily needs as employment opportunities disappear and businesses close.
El Obeid’s once-active industrial sector has been severely affected by disruptions in the supply of agricultural products and prolonged electricity shortages. Most of the city's oil-processing factories have suspended operations, leaving many workers without income.
Recent drone attacks on fuel facilities have further worsened the crisis, causing severe fuel shortages and driving prices sharply higher on the black market.
As conflict continues to disrupt livelihoods and humanitarian access, aid agencies warn that the needs of displaced communities are increasing rapidly, placing additional strain on the city's already overstretched resources.

title: Border Closures Send Sorghum Prices Plunging, Farmers Face Heavy Losses
excerpt: Rutshuru, North Kivu, July 9, 2026 - Sorghum producers in the Jomba area of Rutshuru Territory are facing growing economic difficulties as the price of their harvest drops sharply following the disruption of small-scale cross-border trade with Uganda and Rwanda. Farmers…
title_en: Border Closures Send Sorghum Prices Plunging, Farmers Face Heavy Losses
excerpt_en: Rutshuru, North Kivu, July 9, 2026 - Sorghum producers in the Jomba area of Rutshuru Territory are facing growing economic difficulties as the price of their harvest drops sharply following the disruption of small-scale cross-border trade with Uganda and Rwanda. Farmers…
body_en:
Rutshuru, North Kivu, July 9, 2026 - Sorghum producers in the Jomba area of Rutshuru Territory are facing growing economic difficulties as the price of their harvest drops sharply following the disruption of small-scale cross-border trade with Uganda and Rwanda.
Farmers attribute the decline to border closures introduced as part of measures linked to the Ebola virus disease outbreak, which have significantly reduced the movement of traders who traditionally purchase local agricultural products.
Currently, a measure of sorghum weighing approximately 1.5 kilograms sells for between 2,000 and 2,500 Ugandan shillings, compared with 3,000 Ugandan shillings before the restrictions. Despite a good harvest this season, producers say they are struggling to find buyers and are being forced to sell at prices that do not cover their production costs.
In Tshengerero, farmer Vianney Rwakabuba Rumaka explained that the main challenge is not production but the lack of access to markets. According to him, traders from neighboring countries are no longer crossing the border, leaving farmers with limited opportunities to sell their crops.
He warned that the price collapse is directly affecting the income of farming households, reducing their ability to meet basic needs and reinvest in agricultural activities.
Farmers say the decline represents a major loss compared with previous years, when sorghum sales provided enough income to purchase essential goods. They now fear that an otherwise successful agricultural season could become a financial setback for many rural families.
Producers in Jomba are calling on local and national authorities to take urgent measures to restore trade flows, support market access, or create alternative commercial opportunities to prevent further losses.
The situation highlights the economic vulnerability of communities in eastern DRC, where many rural households depend on cross-border trade networks to sell agricultural products and sustain their livelihoods.

title: Government Launches Biometric Identification of National Police Officers
excerpt: Kinshasa, July 9, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has entered a new phase in the reform of its security sector with the launch of a nationwide biometric identification program for personnel of the Congolese National Police (PNC). The initiative was officially launched…
title_en: Government Launches Biometric Identification of National Police Officers
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, July 9, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has entered a new phase in the reform of its security sector with the launch of a nationwide biometric identification program for personnel of the Congolese National Police (PNC). The initiative was officially launched…
body_en:
Kinshasa, July 9, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has entered a new phase in the reform of its security sector with the launch of a nationwide biometric identification program for personnel of the Congolese National Police (PNC).
The initiative was officially launched on Thursday, July 9, by Jacquemain Shabani Lukoo Bihango, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of the Interior, Security, Decentralization, and Customary Affairs. The operation aims to improve personnel management, strengthen transparency, and modernize the administration of the national police force.
The biometric registration follows the completion of an analysis of the PNC personnel database. The process will begin in Kinshasa as a pilot phase before being gradually extended to all 26 provinces of the country.
The implementation will be carried out by Africa Business Agency (ABA) in cooperation with PNC structures.
According to the Ministry of the Interior, the new system will establish a secure and centralized database of police officers, helping authorities identify and remove duplicate records, detect ghost employees, improve salary management, and strengthen recruitment, deployment, and promotion procedures.
During the launch ceremony, Claude Kikoka Mbala, Chairman of the Board of Directors of Africa Business Agency, presented the audit report on the PNC workforce to Minister Jacquemain Shabani. The document will serve as the foundation for the biometric identification process nationwide.
The reform is part of broader government efforts to professionalize the Congolese National Police, improve institutional efficiency, and strengthen accountability within the security sector.
The ceremony was attended by senior government officials, including Deputy Prime Minister in charge of Budget Adolphe Muzito, Deputy Prime Minister for Civil Service Jean-Pierre Lihau, and Deputy Minister of Finance Gracia Yamba Kazadi.

The ceremony was attended by senior government officials, including Deputy Prime Minister in charge of Budget Adolphe Muzito, Deputy Prime Minister for Civil Service Jean-Pierre Lihau, and Deputy Minister of Finance Gracia Yamba Kazadi.

title: RSF Reinforces Positions Around Kulbus Amid Fears of New Offensive
excerpt: KULBUS, July 9, 2026 - Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have deployed significant military reinforcements around the town of Kulbus in West Darfur, raising fears of an imminent large-scale offensive as fighting intensifies in the region. The military buildup comes less than…
title_en: RSF Reinforces Positions Around Kulbus Amid Fears of New Offensive
excerpt_en: KULBUS, July 9, 2026 - Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have deployed significant military reinforcements around the town of Kulbus in West Darfur, raising fears of an imminent large-scale offensive as fighting intensifies in the region. The military buildup comes less than…
body_en:
KULBUS, July 9, 2026 - Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have deployed significant military reinforcements around the town of Kulbus in West Darfur, raising fears of an imminent large-scale offensive as fighting intensifies in the region.
The military buildup comes less than two weeks after forces allied with the Sudanese army announced they had regained control of Kulbus following heavy clashes with the RSF. The town had been under RSF control since October 2024.
Large convoys of combat vehicles and armoured units have reportedly been moved from El Geneina toward northern parts of West Darfur, while additional reinforcements have arrived from Saraf Omra and Kabkabiya in neighbouring North Darfur.
Military movements have also been observed toward Abu Liha, Abu Qamra, and Wadi Seira, with reports indicating preparations for coordinated operations targeting Kulbus in West Darfur and Tine in North Darfur.
The escalating military activity has forced civilians to flee several villages along the route between Um Baru and Tine after homes, markets, and water facilities were reportedly destroyed during the advance.
Additional RSF forces have taken positions south of Jebel Moon and in the Halilat area, approximately 30 kilometres east of Kulbus, further increasing concerns over a renewed assault on the town.
Located about 130 kilometres north of El Geneina, Kulbus is the historical stronghold of the Gimir community and the seat of its traditional sultanate. During the early stages of the conflict, local leaders had negotiated arrangements that spared the town from major attacks, but Kulbus eventually fell to RSF forces in October 2024 before being recaptured by army-aligned forces in late June 2026.

title: Onion Traders Resist Market Relocation Over Infrastructure Concerns
excerpt: NTUNGAMO, July 9, 2026 - Onion traders in Rwentobo-Rwahi Town Council have opposed plans to relocate them to a new market site in Katooma, warning that poor infrastructure, difficult terrain and limited basic services could disrupt one of western Uganda’s largest produce…
title_en: Onion Traders Resist Market Relocation Over Infrastructure Concerns
excerpt_en: NTUNGAMO, July 9, 2026 - Onion traders in Rwentobo-Rwahi Town Council have opposed plans to relocate them to a new market site in Katooma, warning that poor infrastructure, difficult terrain and limited basic services could disrupt one of western Uganda’s largest produce…
body_en:
NTUNGAMO, July 9, 2026 - Onion traders in Rwentobo-Rwahi Town Council have opposed plans to relocate them to a new market site in Katooma, warning that poor infrastructure, difficult terrain and limited basic services could disrupt one of western Uganda’s largest produce trading centres.
The traders have been directed to vacate their current market by August and move to the new location, but they argue that the proposed site is unsuitable due to its steep landscape, poor road access, insecurity concerns and inadequate sanitation facilities.
Rwentobo-Rwahi has for years served as a major onion collection hub, attracting farmers, buyers and traders from Ntungamo, Kabale, Kisoro, Rukiga and neighbouring districts. The market supplies onions to different parts of Uganda and neighbouring countries, supporting the livelihoods of more than 1,000 people.
Traders say relocating the market could increase transport costs and affect the movement of trucks carrying produce from farms to major markets, including Kampala.
They also argue that the hilly nature of the new site will make it difficult to construct storage facilities and create challenges for loading and offloading vehicles.
Some traders have started moving to the new location in phases despite their concerns. However, they maintain that the relocation process lacked sufficient consultation and could negatively affect business operations.
Local authorities acknowledged challenges at the new site, including limited electricity, poor sanitation and difficult terrain, but said the available land remains the only option to accommodate the growing onion trade.
Officials said improvements to roads and sanitation facilities would be implemented gradually as traders settle at the new market.
The relocation is intended to improve market organisation, prevent unplanned construction of storage facilities and support better physical planning in the growing trading centre.
Authorities said the expansion of onion business activities requires a larger and more organised market space, adding that the transition would be carried out in phases while infrastructure improvements continue.

title: US Calls for Stronger Global Action Against Conflict-Related Sexual Violence in Eastern DRC
excerpt: New York, July 9, 2026 - The United States has urged UN member states to strengthen accountability measures against perpetrators of conflict-related sexual violence, particularly in regions affected by armed conflicts such as eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Speaking…
title_en: US Calls for Stronger Global Action Against Conflict-Related Sexual Violence in Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: New York, July 9, 2026 - The United States has urged UN member states to strengthen accountability measures against perpetrators of conflict-related sexual violence, particularly in regions affected by armed conflicts such as eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Speaking…
body_en:
New York, July 9, 2026 - The United States has urged UN member states to strengthen accountability measures against perpetrators of conflict-related sexual violence, particularly in regions affected by armed conflicts such as eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Speaking during a United Nations Security Council session on Women, Peace and Security held on Wednesday, July 8, U.S. Deputy Representative to the UN Ambassador Tammy Bruce called for concrete actions to prevent sexual violence, support survivors, and ensure that those responsible are brought to justice.
The meeting, focused on protecting victims of conflict-related sexual violence and reinforcing international legal commitments, provided an opportunity for member states to discuss mechanisms to address one of the most persistent consequences of armed conflicts worldwide.
Ambassador Bruce emphasized that international commitments must be followed by practical measures, noting that preventing abuses requires collective action from governments and institutions.
She highlighted recent U.S. sanctions targeting commanders from armed groups operating in eastern DRC, including figures linked to AFC/M23 and FDLR, accused of serious human rights violations, including sexual violence.
The American diplomat called on other countries to adopt similar accountability measures and strengthen their own legal mechanisms to ensure that perpetrators of conflict-related sexual violence face consequences.
According to Bruce, violence against women and children cannot be considered an unavoidable consequence of war. She stressed that international institutions have the capacity and responsibility to move beyond declarations and implement effective solutions.
The discussion comes amid continued reports of sexual violence affecting women and girls in conflict zones, particularly in eastern DRC, where armed groups and ongoing military confrontations have increased civilian vulnerability.
Congolese authorities continue to accuse the AFC/M23 rebellion, which they describe as supported by Rwanda, of contributing to instability and worsening humanitarian conditions in the east of the country.
Despite ongoing diplomatic efforts, including regional and international peace initiatives, violence continues in several areas. While negotiations have produced political commitments, the situation on the ground remains fragile, with armed actors continuing hostilities and accusing one another of failing to respect agreed measures.
The United States said it would continue advocating for stronger international action to protect survivors and prevent sexual violence during conflicts, emphasizing that accountability remains essential for lasting peace.

title: Former FDLR Fighter Reveals Group’s Influence in Eastern DRC Governance
excerpt: KIGALI, July 9, 2026 - Former members of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) have revealed details about alleged abuses within the armed group, including claims that its fighters have influenced local political processes in parts of eastern Democratic…
title_en: Former FDLR Fighter Reveals Group’s Influence in Eastern DRC Governance
excerpt_en: KIGALI, July 9, 2026 - Former members of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) have revealed details about alleged abuses within the armed group, including claims that its fighters have influenced local political processes in parts of eastern Democratic…
body_en:
KIGALI, July 9, 2026 - Former members of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) have revealed details about alleged abuses within the armed group, including claims that its fighters have influenced local political processes in parts of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The testimonies were presented on June 12, 2026, at the Mutobo Demobilization Center during a discussion on the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi. The event, organized by the Unity Club Intwararumuri Association, focused on accounts from former members of armed groups operating in eastern DRC, particularly the FDLR.
Col. (Rtd) Augustin Nshimiyimana, also known as Bora Manassé, a former FDLR member, said he fled Rwanda in 1994 and joined armed groups in the DRC, where he later worked in the group’s intelligence structures.
He said the extremist ideology within the FDLR remains difficult to eliminate because it was transferred from Rwanda into the DRC, where the group established networks and continued its activities.
Nshimiyimana also claimed that the FDLR has become deeply embedded in some local governance structures in eastern DRC, particularly in South Kivu, where he alleged that the group has influenced the selection of political representatives.
According to his testimony, FDLR commanders operating near polling areas have allegedly used their influence to mobilize voters and support preferred candidates during elections, resulting in the group gaining representation in provincial and national institutions.
The former fighter argued that eliminating the FDLR requires more than military action, saying the group has developed political and social networks beyond its armed structures.
The FDLR, which emerged after the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi and is based mainly in eastern DRC, has remained a major security concern in the Great Lakes region. The group has been accused of maintaining extremist networks, spreading hate ideology, and contributing to instability in eastern Congo.
The military wing of the FDLR, known as FDLR-FOCA, is reportedly led by Pacifique Ntawunga, also known as General Omega. Other senior figures include Maj. Gen. Cyprien Uzabakiriho, known as Ave Maria, who previously commanded the group.
The intelligence branch (G2) is reportedly headed by Brig. Gen. Sébastien Uwimbabazi, also known as Nyembo Abdallah, who coordinates operations in areas including Masisi and Walikale. The military operations branch (G3) is led by Brig. Gen. Lucien Nzabanita, while the Special Operations Command (CRAP) is commanded by Col. Pierre-Célestin Rurakabije, also known as Simba Guillaume.
Security assessments indicate that by June 2025, the FDLR’s armed strength was estimated at between 7,000 and 10,000 fighters, maintaining its presence as one of the longstanding armed groups operating in eastern DRC.

title: Rwandan Foreign Minister Pays Tribute to Victims of October 7 Attack in Israel
excerpt: RE'IM, Israel, July 9, 2026 - Rwanda's Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, visited the Nova music festival memorial site in southern Israel to pay tribute to the victims of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack. The visit…
title_en: Rwandan Foreign Minister Pays Tribute to Victims of October 7 Attack in Israel
excerpt_en: RE'IM, Israel, July 9, 2026 - Rwanda's Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, visited the Nova music festival memorial site in southern Israel to pay tribute to the victims of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack. The visit…
body_en:
RE'IM, Israel, July 9, 2026 - Rwanda's Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, visited the Nova music festival memorial site in southern Israel to pay tribute to the victims of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack.
The visit took place at the memorial in Re'im, where hundreds of people attending the Nova music festival were killed during the attack. Rwanda's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the visit was intended to honor the victims and commemorate those who lost their lives in the assault.
The visit comes as Rwanda and Israel continue to strengthen bilateral relations, with both countries frequently highlighting the importance of combating hatred, violence, and attacks against civilians while drawing lessons from their respective historical tragedies.
The October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, which involved assaults on civilian communities and the Nova music festival near the Gaza border, triggered the ongoing conflict between Israel and Hamas. The war has since resulted in significant humanitarian and security challenges across the region.

title: Uganda Pushes for Commercialisation of Home-Grown Infrastructure Innovations
excerpt: KAMPALA, July 9, 2026 - Uganda is seeking to accelerate the transition of scientific research from laboratories into communities and industries, with the government emphasising the commercialisation of locally developed technologies to address infrastructure challenges. The…
title_en: Uganda Pushes for Commercialisation of Home-Grown Infrastructure Innovations
excerpt_en: KAMPALA, July 9, 2026 - Uganda is seeking to accelerate the transition of scientific research from laboratories into communities and industries, with the government emphasising the commercialisation of locally developed technologies to address infrastructure challenges. The…
body_en:
KAMPALA, July 9, 2026 - Uganda is seeking to accelerate the transition of scientific research from laboratories into communities and industries, with the government emphasising the commercialisation of locally developed technologies to address infrastructure challenges.
The Minister of Science, Technology and Innovation Jonard Asiimwe said research and innovation must deliver practical solutions that improve public services, increase productivity and support industrial development.
He said the government is working to strengthen partnerships between researchers, universities, industry players and the private sector to ensure locally developed technologies move from concept stages into real-world applications.
Asiimwe stressed that innovation should not remain limited to academic institutions but should be deployed in communities, industries and public systems where it can directly improve livelihoods.
The government is also increasing focus on research and development investment as part of efforts to build a competitive, resilient and self-reliant economy driven by science, technology and innovation.
The initiative forms part of a broader strategy to promote home-grown solutions and reduce dependence on imported technologies while supporting Uganda’s industrial transformation agenda.

title: Fragile Calm Returns to Kalembe and Kalonge After Night of Fighting Between AFC/M23 and Wazalendo
excerpt: Goma, July 9, 2026 - A fragile calm has returned to Kalembe and Kalonge, two localities located along the border between Masisi and Walikale territories in North Kivu, following a night of intense clashes between AFC/M23 fighters and Wazalendo armed groups. The fighting…
title_en: Fragile Calm Returns to Kalembe and Kalonge After Night of Fighting Between AFC/M23 and Wazalendo
excerpt_en: Goma, July 9, 2026 - A fragile calm has returned to Kalembe and Kalonge, two localities located along the border between Masisi and Walikale territories in North Kivu, following a night of intense clashes between AFC/M23 fighters and Wazalendo armed groups. The fighting…
body_en:
Goma, July 9, 2026 - A fragile calm has returned to Kalembe and Kalonge, two localities located along the border between Masisi and Walikale territories in North Kivu, following a night of intense clashes between AFC/M23 fighters and Wazalendo armed groups.
The fighting erupted late Wednesday, July 8, around 11:00 p.m., according to local sources, after Wazalendo forces launched an attack against AFC/M23 positions in the area. Exchanges of fire involving heavy and light weapons continued for several hours until around 4:00 a.m. Thursday, causing widespread fear among residents.
Several inhabitants reported spending the night sheltering inside their homes as explosions and gunfire echoed across the area. Some families sought refuge at the Kalembe health center, considered a safer location during the confrontation.
“We spent the night at the health center because the fighting was coming from several directions,” one resident said, describing the panic caused by the intensity of the clashes.
According to traditional authorities, Wazalendo fighters withdrew from Kalembe after several hours of combat. Since Thursday morning, the situation has remained relatively calm, allowing some displaced residents to gradually return home.
However, the atmosphere remains tense, with many residents reluctant to resume normal activities due to fears that fighting could resume at any moment.
Local authorities and community leaders are continuing to monitor developments, while assessments are underway to determine possible casualties and material damage. No official figures have been released so far.
The latest clashes highlight the persistent insecurity in the border areas between Masisi and Walikale, where confrontations between armed groups continue to threaten civilian populations and complicate efforts to restore lasting stability in North Kivu.

title: Illegal Poaching Threatens Rwanda’s Wildlife and Public Health
excerpt: Nyamasheke, July 9, 2026 - Rwandan authorities have warned that crimes committed in national parks pose risks beyond environmental destruction, emphasizing that illegal hunting and unauthorized entry into protected areas can increase the spread of zoonotic diseases such as…
title_en: Illegal Poaching Threatens Rwanda’s Wildlife and Public Health
excerpt_en: Nyamasheke, July 9, 2026 - Rwandan authorities have warned that crimes committed in national parks pose risks beyond environmental destruction, emphasizing that illegal hunting and unauthorized entry into protected areas can increase the spread of zoonotic diseases such as...
body_en:
Nyamasheke, July 9, 2026 - Rwandan authorities have warned that crimes committed in national parks pose risks beyond environmental destruction, emphasizing that illegal hunting and unauthorized entry into protected areas can increase the spread of zoonotic diseases such as Ebola, Marburg and mpox.

Officials reported that since 2020, hundreds of suspects have been arrested for damaging Nyungwe National Park, but many are released before trial. They argued that environmental crimes are often treated too lightly despite their lasting impact on endangered wildlife and fragile ecosystems.

Authorities stressed that contact between humans and wild animals can facilitate the transmission of infectious diseases, noting that many major outbreaks originate from wildlife.

They called for stronger enforcement of environmental laws and greater recognition of the importance of protecting Rwanda’s national parks for biodiversity, public health and sustainable development.

The developments were reported in the RWANDA briefing covering mid-to-late July 2026. The account centers on: Illegal Poaching Threatens Rwanda’s Wildlife and Public Health. Taken together, the available details outline both the immediate incident and the broader situation described by officials and witnesses in the source report.

excerpt: BRUSSELS, July 9, 2026 - The European Parliament has adopted a resolution calling on the European Union to designate Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF) as a terrorist organization and expand sanctions against individuals and entities linked to attacks on civilians during the…
title_en: European Parliament Urges EU to List Sudan’s RSF as Terrorist Organization
excerpt_en: BRUSSELS, July 9, 2026 - The European Parliament has adopted a resolution calling on the European Union to designate Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF) as a terrorist organization and expand sanctions against individuals and entities linked to attacks on civilians during the…
body_en:
BRUSSELS, July 9, 2026 - The European Parliament has adopted a resolution calling on the European Union to designate Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF) as a terrorist organization and expand sanctions against individuals and entities linked to attacks on civilians during the ongoing conflict.
The resolution, approved by a large majority of lawmakers, also calls for sanctions against those accused of facilitating violence against civilians, including a company based in the United Arab Emirates alleged to have violated the United Nations arms embargo on Darfur.
Members of the European Parliament urged the EU to strengthen accountability measures, support independent investigations into alleged war crimes, and encourage broader jurisdiction for the International Criminal Court to investigate violations committed across Sudan.
The resolution expressed particular concern over the humanitarian situation in El-Obeid, where continued fighting and the threat of a large-scale assault have placed hundreds of thousands of civilians and displaced people at risk.
Lawmakers strongly condemned attacks on civilians, including reported incidents of sexual violence, and called on all parties to the conflict to respect international humanitarian law and end actions contributing to famine and humanitarian suffering.
The European Parliament also condemned foreign involvement that could be fueling the conflict and called on all countries to cease any form of military or logistical support to the RSF, including the transfer of weapons.
In addition to tougher sanctions, the resolution urged the European Union to increase humanitarian assistance to Sudan, provide greater support to local relief organizations-particularly those delivering healthcare-and establish secure humanitarian corridors to facilitate civilian evacuations and the delivery of emergency aid.

title: Sudan Launches 3 Trillion-Pound Fund to Support Summer Farming Season
excerpt: KHARTOUM, July 9, 2026 - Sudan’s government has approved the creation of a banking finance fund worth more than 3 trillion Sudanese pounds to support the 2026 summer agricultural season and strengthen financing for the country’s productive sectors. The initiative comes as…
title_en: Sudan Launches 3 Trillion-Pound Fund to Support Summer Farming Season
excerpt_en: KHARTOUM, July 9, 2026 - Sudan’s government has approved the creation of a banking finance fund worth more than 3 trillion Sudanese pounds to support the 2026 summer agricultural season and strengthen financing for the country’s productive sectors. The initiative comes as…
body_en:
KHARTOUM, July 9, 2026 - Sudan’s government has approved the creation of a banking finance fund worth more than 3 trillion Sudanese pounds to support the 2026 summer agricultural season and strengthen financing for the country’s productive sectors.
The initiative comes as farmers face mounting challenges caused by the ongoing conflict, including limited access to financing, shortages of improved seeds and fertilizers, rising fuel prices, and disrupted supply chains.
Finance Minister Gibril Ibrahim said the fund is designed to ensure the success of the July-to-October farming season. He also announced that the government will cover a substantial share of agricultural insurance costs to reduce financial pressure on farmers.
The minister encouraged the formation of agricultural cooperatives to help small-scale producers gain easier access to financing, technical support, agricultural extension services, and essential production inputs.
The financing initiative was approved following consultations involving the finance ministry, the Central Bank of Sudan, the Agricultural Bank, and commercial banks.
Under the plan, the Central Bank will contribute 20% of the fund’s value, while each commercial bank will provide at least 5% of the targeted financing. The programme is intended to expand investment in agriculture while safeguarding participating banks' capital and returns, with particular emphasis on microfinance and strengthening agricultural value chains from production to export.
The government aims to cultivate 1.2 million feddans in the Gezira Scheme, 7.6 million feddans in Gedaref State, and more than 3.3 million feddans in White Nile State during the current season.
Agriculture remains a cornerstone of Sudan’s economy, employing around 80% of the workforce and contributing nearly 32% of the country’s gross domestic product. However, agricultural output has declined significantly in recent years as conflict, rising production costs, and adverse weather conditions continue to affect food production and rural livelihoods.

title: Rwanda Warns Minimum Wage Increase Could Trigger Job Losses Without Productivity Growth
excerpt: KIGALI, July 9, 2026 - Rwanda’s Prime Minister Dr. Justin Nsengiyumva has called for caution in discussions over introducing a national minimum wage, warning that a poorly designed policy could increase unemployment if businesses are unable to absorb higher labor costs.…
title_en: Rwanda Warns Minimum Wage Increase Could Trigger Job Losses Without Productivity Growth
excerpt_en: KIGALI, July 9, 2026 - Rwanda’s Prime Minister Dr. Justin Nsengiyumva has called for caution in discussions over introducing a national minimum wage, warning that a poorly designed policy could increase unemployment if businesses are unable to absorb higher labor costs.…
body_en:
KIGALI, July 9, 2026 - Rwanda’s Prime Minister Dr. Justin Nsengiyumva has called for caution in discussions over introducing a national minimum wage, warning that a poorly designed policy could increase unemployment if businesses are unable to absorb higher labor costs.
Addressing Parliament on June 9, 2026, while presenting the government’s efforts to strengthen economic capacity and improve citizens’ welfare, the Prime Minister said increasing productivity and workers’ incomes should remain a priority rather than imposing a minimum wage without considering economic realities.
Rwanda’s current minimum wage dates back to 1974 and sets a daily payment of 100 Rwandan francs for employees working for others.
Dr. Nsengiyumva said wage discussions should distinguish between a basic salary and a living wage that enables workers to support their families, cover essential needs, and maintain a decent standard of living.
He argued that employers must also be considered in any wage reform because salaries are paid from business revenues.
The Prime Minister gave the example of a company employing 10 workers at 50,000 Rwandan francs each per month, saying that forcing the employer to double salaries without a corresponding increase in income could make it impossible to maintain the same workforce.
He warned that although a minimum wage law may appear beneficial, it could fail in practice if employers lack the financial capacity to comply.
According to him, some businesses could respond to higher wage requirements by reducing staff numbers, turning a policy intended to improve workers’ lives into a source of unemployment.
Dr. Nsengiyumva said the issue requires broad discussion that balances workers’ living conditions with the ability of businesses and industries to sustain employment.
He acknowledged that some sectors still pay very low wages, including workers earning around 1,500 Rwandan francs, and said the government is working to address these gaps.
The government has also focused on ensuring that funds allocated for daily workers’ salaries in development projects are fully paid to employees rather than being reduced through intermediaries.
Since the first quarter of 2025, Rwanda has recorded the creation of more than 240,000 jobs as part of efforts to expand employment opportunities and strengthen household incomes.
Justice and Rights

title: Sudan and African Union Discuss Return of Khartoum Liaison Office Amid Peace Efforts
excerpt: KHARTOUM, July 9, 2026 - Sudan’s Sovereign Council Chairman and army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has held talks with African Union envoy Mohamed Belaiche on efforts to advance peace, address obstacles to negotiations, and prepare for the reopening of the AU liaison office in…
title_en: Sudan and African Union Discuss Return of Khartoum Liaison Office Amid Peace Efforts
excerpt_en: KHARTOUM, July 9, 2026 - Sudan’s Sovereign Council Chairman and army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has held talks with African Union envoy Mohamed Belaiche on efforts to advance peace, address obstacles to negotiations, and prepare for the reopening of the AU liaison office in…
body_en:
KHARTOUM, July 9, 2026 - Sudan’s Sovereign Council Chairman and army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has held talks with African Union envoy Mohamed Belaiche on efforts to advance peace, address obstacles to negotiations, and prepare for the reopening of the AU liaison office in Khartoum.
The meeting, attended by Foreign Minister Mohieddin Salem, focused on the security and political situation in Sudan, as well as practical arrangements for restoring the African Union’s presence in the country.
Belaiche said the discussions examined ways to overcome challenges hindering peace efforts and stressed the importance of strengthening initiatives aimed at achieving stability and security.
The AU envoy reaffirmed the bloc’s commitment to supporting de-escalation and said a ceasefire remains the key step toward addressing the crisis, alongside an inclusive political process involving Sudanese stakeholders.
The African Union is leading mediation efforts through a broader international mechanism that includes the United Nations, European Union, IGAD, and the Arab League. The initiative aims to bring Sudanese political and military actors together to discuss the country’s future governance.
The mechanism has received international backing, particularly after Sudanese political groups reached preliminary understandings on elements of a future political process, including the creation of a joint committee. However, disagreements remain over the participation of some groups, including the Islamic Movement and the “Taasis” coalition.
A new round of consultations between political forces is expected later this month as regional and international actors continue efforts to find a negotiated solution to Sudan’s conflict.
The African Union said it remains committed to supporting Sudan’s unity, sovereignty, and national reconciliation while monitoring political, security, and humanitarian developments.
A high-level AU delegation is also expected to visit Khartoum as part of ongoing diplomatic engagement.
Sudan’s membership in the African Union has remained suspended since the October 2021 military coup, with the bloc linking its return to the formation of a civilian-led government.

title: President Kagame Joins Global Leaders in Geneva to Shape Future of Artificial Intelligence
excerpt: GENEVA, Switzerland, July 8, 2026 - President Paul Kagame has joined global leaders and technology experts at the AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva, where discussions are focused on ensuring artificial intelligence serves humanity and helps reduce technological inequalities…
title_en: President Kagame Joins Global Leaders in Geneva to Shape Future of Artificial Intelligence
excerpt_en: GENEVA, Switzerland, July 8, 2026 - President Paul Kagame has joined global leaders and technology experts at the AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva, where discussions are focused on ensuring artificial intelligence serves humanity and helps reduce technological inequalities…
body_en:
GENEVA, Switzerland, July 8, 2026 - President Paul Kagame has joined global leaders and technology experts at the AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva, where discussions are focused on ensuring artificial intelligence serves humanity and helps reduce technological inequalities worldwide.
The summit, organized by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) in partnership with Switzerland and other United Nations bodies, is taking place from July 7 to 10, 2026. It brings together governments, international organizations, technology companies, and researchers to explore ways of developing and using AI responsibly.
President Kagame addressed participants during the opening session and took part in the launch of a new global commission on artificial intelligence. He will co-chair the commission alongside Salesforce CEO and co-founder Marc Benioff, with ITU Secretary-General Doreen Bogdan-Martin serving as deputy chair.
The commission will bring together political leaders, AI developers, and industry experts to develop a shared vision for the responsible use of artificial intelligence. Its priorities include improving trust in AI systems, expanding access for developing countries, strengthening digital infrastructure, building human capacity, and reducing the technology gap between nations.
The summit comes amid growing global debate over AI's opportunities and risks. While the technology is being applied in sectors such as healthcare, education, agriculture, public services, and security, experts have raised concerns about misinformation, cybersecurity threats, economic inequality, and the exclusion of countries lacking the resources to adopt and regulate AI.
Rwanda's participation reflects its long-term focus on technology as a driver of development. The country has promoted digital innovation, expanded technology-based services, and invested in building skills among young people as part of its broader development strategy.

title: Kampala Police Urge Community Cooperation to Combat Crime and Drug Abuse
excerpt: Kampala, Uganda, July 8, 2026 - Police authorities have called on residents across the Kampala Metropolitan area to strengthen cooperation with security agencies in efforts to combat crime and drug abuse, emphasizing that community participation remains essential to…
title_en: Kampala Police Urge Community Cooperation to Combat Crime and Drug Abuse
excerpt_en: Kampala, Uganda, July 8, 2026 - Police authorities have called on residents across the Kampala Metropolitan area to strengthen cooperation with security agencies in efforts to combat crime and drug abuse, emphasizing that community participation remains essential to…
body_en:
Kampala, Uganda, July 8, 2026 - Police authorities have called on residents across the Kampala Metropolitan area to strengthen cooperation with security agencies in efforts to combat crime and drug abuse, emphasizing that community participation remains essential to maintaining public safety.
During a security engagement with residents and local leaders, Kampala Metropolitan Police Commander ACP Ezekiel Emitu Ebapu said the security situation in the capital remains generally stable despite isolated incidents, including house break-ins, theft, bag snatching, muggings, and land-related disputes.
Authorities noted that land conflicts have become increasingly common, particularly in Kawempe and Wakiso, as rising property values continue to fuel ownership disputes.
Police also expressed concern over the growing involvement of young people in criminal activities, attributing much of the trend to the abuse of illicit drugs. Recent security operations have resulted in the seizure of substances including marijuana and opium, which authorities say contribute to criminal behaviour by impairing judgment.
Residents, parents, and community leaders were encouraged to play a more active role in preventing youth from becoming involved in crime and to report suspected offenders to law enforcement. Police stressed that effective crime prevention depends on timely information from local communities.
The engagement also served as an opportunity for police to assess public security concerns and gather feedback on improving policing services across the metropolitan area.
Authorities further encouraged citizens to participate in the upcoming Local Council One (LC1) elections, stressing the importance of electing responsible local leaders capable of working with communities and security agencies to promote peace, security, and local development.

title: DRC Strengthens Anti-Corruption Framework as Government and Private Sector Join Forces on New Law
excerpt: Kinshasa, July 8, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo is advancing efforts to strengthen its legal framework against corruption, with the government and private sector reaffirming their commitment to closer cooperation in promoting transparency and good governance. A…
title_en: DRC Strengthens Anti-Corruption Framework as Government and Private Sector Join Forces on New Law
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, July 8, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo is advancing efforts to strengthen its legal framework against corruption, with the government and private sector reaffirming their commitment to closer cooperation in promoting transparency and good governance. A…
body_en:
Kinshasa, July 8, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo is advancing efforts to strengthen its legal framework against corruption, with the government and private sector reaffirming their commitment to closer cooperation in promoting transparency and good governance.
A working session held in Kinshasa on July 7 brought together the Ministry of Justice, the United Nations Global Compact Network in the DRC, and private sector representatives under the leadership of Minister of State, Minister of Justice and Keeper of the Seals, Guillaume Ngefa.
The meeting focused on the latest developments in the draft anti-corruption law recently adopted by the Council of Ministers, including technical adjustments made to the text and preparations for its broader dissemination among stakeholders.
Jessica Webe, Executive Director of the UN Global Compact Network DRC, welcomed the progress achieved, noting that around 75 percent of recommendations submitted by the organization's anti-corruption commission had been integrated into the draft law following months of consultations with government authorities.
Private sector representatives also expressed support for the reform. Hugues Boketsu Efole, Deputy Managing Director of Equity BCDC and head of the UN Global Compact's anti-corruption commission on a rotating basis, said businesses are committed to contributing to the creation of a more transparent economic environment and strengthening trust between institutions and companies.
As part of the implementation process, stakeholders announced plans to launch awareness campaigns targeting businesses and civil society organizations to promote understanding of the new legal framework and encourage effective compliance.
Adopted by the Council of Ministers on June 26 under the chairmanship of President Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi Tshilombo, the draft law seeks to modernize the country's approach to fighting corruption through four main pillars: prevention, protection, prosecution, and judicial procedures.
The proposed legislation also introduces measures on international cooperation, recovery of assets obtained through illicit activities, and obligations for companies to establish internal mechanisms to prevent and combat corruption.
The reform comes as the DRC continues to face significant governance challenges, with corruption remaining a major concern in public administration and economic sectors. Authorities argue that the new legal framework will help strengthen accountability mechanisms and improve the country's business climate.
Following its adoption by the government, the bill will now proceed to Parliament for examination by the National Assembly and the Senate before being submitted for presidential promulgation.
Since President Félix Tshisekedi took office, several institutional reforms have been launched, including efforts to strengthen oversight bodies such as the General Inspectorate of Finance (IGF) and the Court of Auditors. However, civil society organizations and economic experts continue to call for stronger enforcement mechanisms and more binding measures to achieve lasting progress in the fight against corruption.

UNITED NATIONS, July 8, 2026 - The United Nations’ envoy for Sudan, Pekka Haavisto, has begun a diplomatic mission to neighbouring Chad to assess the regional consequences of Sudan’s ongoing conflict and seek ways to reduce tensions.
During the visit, Haavisto is holding discussions with Chadian authorities and diplomatic representatives on security developments and the wider impact of the war on neighbouring countries.
The UN envoy is also expected to visit refugee camps hosting thousands of Sudanese civilians who fled the fighting, as humanitarian concerns continue to grow along Sudan’s borders.
The mission comes amid increasing international concern that the conflict, now entering its fourth year, is spreading instability across the region and placing additional pressure on neighbouring states.
Haavisto has been engaging with regional actors as part of efforts to prevent further military escalation and revive political dialogue aimed at achieving a lasting solution to the crisis.
Following his meetings in Chad, the UN envoy is expected to return to Sudan in the coming weeks for discussions with senior government officials.
The visit is part of broader diplomatic efforts involving international and regional organizations, including the United Nations, African Union, Arab League, European Union, and IGAD, to push for de-escalation and renewed negotiations between Sudan’s warring parties.

title: Djibouti's Yellow Kiosks Drive Digital Services and Economic Inclusion
excerpt: Djibouti City, July 8, 2026 - Once symbols of a bygone era of public telecommunications, Djibouti's iconic yellow phone booths have been transformed into digital service kiosks, creating new opportunities for entrepreneurship, financial inclusion, and employment across the…
title_en: Djibouti's Yellow Kiosks Drive Digital Services and Economic Inclusion
excerpt_en: Djibouti City, July 8, 2026 - Once symbols of a bygone era of public telecommunications, Djibouti's iconic yellow phone booths have been transformed into digital service kiosks, creating new opportunities for entrepreneurship, financial inclusion, and employment across the…
body_en:
Djibouti City, July 8, 2026 - Once symbols of a bygone era of public telecommunications, Djibouti's iconic yellow phone booths have been transformed into digital service kiosks, creating new opportunities for entrepreneurship, financial inclusion, and employment across the capital.
Repurposed through a corporate social responsibility initiative involving national and international partners, the former telephone booths now serve as neighborhood service centers offering digital financial transactions, document services, and administrative support to local communities.
Equipped with computers, printers, scanners, photocopiers, and connected to digital payment platforms, the kiosks provide services including electronic money deposits and withdrawals, mobile phone credit sales, printing, photocopying, document scanning, and assistance with administrative procedures. Their growing presence throughout Djibouti City and Balbala has expanded access to essential services while supporting the country's ongoing digital transformation.
Beyond improving public access to digital services, the initiative has created entrepreneurial opportunities for hundreds of young Djiboutians, with particular emphasis on promoting economic inclusion for people with disabilities.
Among the beneficiaries is Houmed Mohamed Ali, an entrepreneur living with a physical disability who now manages one of the kiosks. After completing training in entrepreneurship, business management, and personal development, he launched his business with support from the program. The kiosk has enabled him to generate a stable income while achieving greater financial independence and supporting his family.
Like many other operators, Houmed assists customers with daily digital transactions, including electronic payments, cash transfers, mobile credit purchases, and document services. The expansion of these neighborhood kiosks has significantly reduced the need for residents to travel long distances to access financial and administrative services.
The initiative reflects the rapid growth of digital financial services in Djibouti and demonstrates how technological innovation can be combined with inclusive economic policies to create employment and expand access to essential services.
By transforming obsolete public infrastructure into community business centers, the project has given a second life to the former telephone booths while providing hundreds of entrepreneurs with new economic opportunities. The yellow kiosks have become visible symbols of resilience, digital innovation, and social inclusion, illustrating how public-private collaboration can contribute to sustainable development and improve livelihoods across the country.

title: New Road Taxes Turn Manono-Nyunzu-Kalemie Corridor into Economic Challenge
excerpt: Kalemie, Tanganyika, July 8, 2026 - The reopening of the Manono-Nyunzu-Kalemie road, once viewed as a major opportunity to revive trade and reconnect an isolated part of Tanganyika Province, is now generating growing frustration among transporters, traders, and local…
title_en: New Road Taxes Turn Manono-Nyunzu-Kalemie Corridor into Economic Challenge
excerpt_en: Kalemie, Tanganyika, July 8, 2026 - The reopening of the Manono-Nyunzu-Kalemie road, once viewed as a major opportunity to revive trade and reconnect an isolated part of Tanganyika Province, is now generating growing frustration among transporters, traders, and local…
body_en:
Kalemie, Tanganyika, July 8, 2026 - The reopening of the Manono-Nyunzu-Kalemie road, once viewed as a major opportunity to revive trade and reconnect an isolated part of Tanganyika Province, is now generating growing frustration among transporters, traders, and local residents who accuse authorities of allowing excessive taxation along the strategic route.
The 446-kilometer road was expected to transform economic activity in Manono Territory, which had remained largely cut off for years due to the poor state of transport infrastructure. But according to civil society organizations and traders' representatives, the benefits of improved access are being undermined by the multiplication of tolls, checkpoints, and additional fees imposed on road users.
In a joint statement released on July 7, the Manono Civil Society Coordination and the Manono Traders' Association warned that the financial pressure created by these charges is affecting businesses and increasing the cost of living for households across the province.
Transport Costs Drive Up Prices
According to the organizations, vehicles using the road are subjected to different toll rates depending on their category. Passenger vehicles, medium-sized trucks, and heavy transport vehicles are all required to pay specific charges along the route.
The burden is even greater for trucks transporting goods. Traders say the accumulation of fees has significantly increased the cost of moving essential commodities, creating a domino effect throughout the local economy.
Transport operators raise their prices to cover additional expenses, traders then pass these costs on to consumers, and families ultimately pay more for basic necessities such as flour, sugar, salt, and cooking oil.
“We believed this road would bring relief, but taxation is now becoming unbearable,” a trader from Manono was quoted as saying, warning that many businesses are operating at a loss.
Calls for Government Intervention
Economic actors also denounce the growing number of roadblocks where additional payments are allegedly demanded without clear justification.
Civil society groups are calling on national and provincial authorities to establish a transparent toll system, eliminate abusive practices, clearly define authorized fees, and protect local businesses from excessive financial pressure.
They warn that if the situation continues, the road project could fail to deliver the economic transformation expected by communities that have long suffered from isolation.
A Strategic Corridor for Tanganyika’s Development
The rehabilitation of the Kalemie-Manono road began in October 2024 as part of efforts to open up Tanganyika Province and improve regional connectivity. The route links Kalemie to Manono Territory and connects major national transport corridors.
Provincial authorities have described the project as strategic for economic development, security, and the movement of goods and people across Tanganyika's territories.
The road is also part of a broader cooperation framework between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Tanzania aimed at strengthening the central corridor and expanding commercial exchanges between the two countries.
For residents of Manono, however, the current debate is no longer only about rebuilding roads. It is about ensuring that improved infrastructure translates into real economic relief rather than becoming another source of financial hardship.

title: Dozens of Young People Arrested During AFC/M23 Security Operation Near Katindo Camp
excerpt: Goma, July 8, 2026 - Around fifty young people were arrested on Tuesday, July 7, during a security operation carried out by AFC/M23 police forces near the former Katindo military camp in Goma, North Kivu. According to testimonies collected from relatives and local residents,…
title_en: Dozens of Young People Arrested During AFC/M23 Security Operation Near Katindo Camp
excerpt_en: Goma, July 8, 2026 - Around fifty young people were arrested on Tuesday, July 7, during a security operation carried out by AFC/M23 police forces near the former Katindo military camp in Goma, North Kivu. According to testimonies collected from relatives and local residents,…
body_en:
Goma, July 8, 2026 - Around fifty young people were arrested on Tuesday, July 7, during a security operation carried out by AFC/M23 police forces near the former Katindo military camp in Goma, North Kivu.
According to testimonies collected from relatives and local residents, the arrests took place along Salongo 3 and Katoyi 1 avenues, located between the Mabanga-Nord and Kasika neighborhoods in Karisimbi commune.
Residents said the operation targeted young people who had reportedly been identified by local communities following an increase in theft incidents in the area. Some of those arrested were also accused of consuming marijuana.
Witnesses reported that the individuals were first gathered inside the Katindo military camp before being transported by truck to an unknown location. At this stage, no official communication has been issued regarding their identities, their current whereabouts, or the legal reasons behind their detention.
Some community members are calling for a verification process to distinguish between individuals genuinely suspected of wrongdoing and those who may have been arrested without sufficient evidence.
The arrests come shortly after another security operation conducted in Goma under the AFC/M23 administration, during which several young people were reportedly detained for alleged violations of municipal regulations and charges related to public disorder.
The latest operation occurred as residents across the country were closely following the DRC national football team’s participation in the 2026 FIFA World Cup. While enthusiasm around the competition spread among the population, Goma remained under a strong security presence, with patrols and arrests reported in several neighborhoods.
Earlier, several young people detained during celebrations following the DRC Leopards’ goal against England were released on Friday, July 3, after spending two nights in custody.

title: Displaced Residents Return to Batakirwa Villages Despite Ongoing Security Risks
excerpt: Walikale, July 8, 2026 - After spending more than two weeks hiding in the bush due to armed clashes, residents of several villages in the Batakirwa area of Walikale territory, North Kivu, have begun returning home despite continued security concerns. Since Monday, July 6,…
title_en: Displaced Residents Return to Batakirwa Villages Despite Ongoing Security Risks
excerpt_en: Walikale, July 8, 2026 - After spending more than two weeks hiding in the bush due to armed clashes, residents of several villages in the Batakirwa area of Walikale territory, North Kivu, have begun returning home despite continued security concerns. Since Monday, July 6,…
body_en:
Walikale, July 8, 2026 - After spending more than two weeks hiding in the bush due to armed clashes, residents of several villages in the Batakirwa area of Walikale territory, North Kivu, have begun returning home despite continued security concerns.
Since Monday, July 6, inhabitants of Iseya, Bubere, Buringa, Tusangwa, and Kilambo villages, located in the Bafuna group, have gradually resumed their return after fleeing fighting that erupted on June 18 between two rival factions of the Uhuru DRC armed group.
The clashes, involving forces loyal to Désiré Kashira Mashite and Shimiray Mushunganya Zidane, forced hundreds of civilians to abandon their homes and seek refuge in forested areas, where many lived under extremely difficult conditions.
Returning residents described severe humanitarian hardships during their displacement, including shortages of food, drinking water, medicine, and limited access to healthcare services. Vulnerable groups, particularly children, pregnant women, and elderly people, were among the most affected.
Several returnees said they decided to go back despite the risks because conditions in the bush had become unbearable and returning home offered better opportunities to access farmland and basic resources.
Local administrative authorities confirmed that the difficult living conditions during displacement were the main reason behind the population’s decision to return. According to Bisu Tahiro Clément, administrative secretary of the Bafuna group, many families could no longer survive without access to essential services and agricultural activities.
However, the security situation remains fragile. Fighters from the two opposing Uhuru DRC factions are still reportedly present in some villages, particularly Iseya and Kilambo, raising fears of renewed confrontations.
Despite these risks, many residents have chosen to rebuild their lives and resume farming, their main source of livelihood.
Local authorities are calling on the FARDC to urgently strengthen its presence in Batakirwa to protect civilians, secure villages, and prevent further clashes between the rival armed factions.

title: Ethiopia Rejects Regional Alliance Concerns, Says Sovereignty Is Not at Risk
excerpt: ADDIS ABABA, July 8, 2026 - Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has dismissed concerns over a possible regional alliance involving Eritrea, Sudan, and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), saying Ethiopia is prepared to defend its sovereignty against any threat.…
title_en: Ethiopia Rejects Regional Alliance Concerns, Says Sovereignty Is Not at Risk
excerpt_en: ADDIS ABABA, July 8, 2026 - Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has dismissed concerns over a possible regional alliance involving Eritrea, Sudan, and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), saying Ethiopia is prepared to defend its sovereignty against any threat.…
body_en:
ADDIS ABABA, July 8, 2026 - Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has dismissed concerns over a possible regional alliance involving Eritrea, Sudan, and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), saying Ethiopia is prepared to defend its sovereignty against any threat.
Addressing lawmakers during the 30th regular session of the House of Peoples’ Representatives, Abiy said Ethiopia does not fear any combination of regional actors and is strengthening its defence capabilities to protect national interests.
The prime minister’s comments came after reports by regional analysts suggesting a possible tactical alignment between Eritrea, the TPLF, and Sudan, with some comparisons drawn to past alliances that reshaped Ethiopia’s political landscape.
Tensions across the Horn of Africa have increased in recent months as relations between Ethiopia and several neighbouring countries have deteriorated. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara have become increasingly strained following disagreements over regional influence and Ethiopia’s efforts to secure access to a Red Sea port.
Ethiopia’s ties with Sudan have also been affected by Sudan’s internal conflict. The Sudanese Armed Forces have accused Addis Ababa of supporting the Rapid Support Forces, while Sudan has responded to alleged cross-border security incidents by reinforcing its military presence along the Ethiopian border.
Abiy also claimed that unnamed external actors were attempting to influence regional developments against Ethiopia, without identifying those involved.
The Ethiopian leader reiterated that his government remains committed to protecting the country’s territorial integrity and maintaining national security amid growing regional tensions.

title: Djibouti Expands International Cooperation in the Fight Against Corruption
excerpt: Djibouti City, July 8, 2026 - Djibouti has reinforced its international engagement in the fight against corruption through two high-level missions in West and East Africa, strengthening bilateral partnerships and contributing to regional efforts to promote transparency,…
title_en: Djibouti Expands International Cooperation in the Fight Against Corruption
excerpt_en: Djibouti City, July 8, 2026 - Djibouti has reinforced its international engagement in the fight against corruption through two high-level missions in West and East Africa, strengthening bilateral partnerships and contributing to regional efforts to promote transparency,…
body_en:
Djibouti City, July 8, 2026 - Djibouti has reinforced its international engagement in the fight against corruption through two high-level missions in West and East Africa, strengthening bilateral partnerships and contributing to regional efforts to promote transparency, accountability, and good governance.
The Independent National Commission for the Prevention and Fight against Corruption (CNIPLC) carried out parallel missions in Côte d'Ivoire and Madagascar, reflecting the country's strategy of enhancing institutional cooperation, sharing expertise, and supporting the implementation of international anti-corruption standards.
From July 1 to 3, a Djiboutian delegation led by CNIPLC President Badria Zakaria Cheik Ibrahim visited Abidjan for discussions with Côte d'Ivoire's High Authority for Good Governance. The mission focused on exchanging experiences and identifying best practices for preventing corruption and strengthening institutional integrity.
The discussions covered a range of governance tools, including compliance assessment systems, public administration performance evaluation, anti-corruption awareness campaigns, perception surveys, and institutional mechanisms designed to improve transparency and accountability within public institutions.
During the visit, the delegation also met representatives of Côte d'Ivoire's Economic and Financial Criminal Unit and the General Confederation of Businesses of Côte d'Ivoire to explore cooperation on judicial coordination, private sector integrity, and corruption risk prevention.
The mission concluded with the signing of a partnership agreement between the two anti-corruption institutions, establishing a framework for long-term collaboration through joint activities, knowledge exchange, and institutional capacity building.
At the same time, another CNIPLC delegation participated in a United Nations review mission in Antananarivo from June 30 to July 2 as part of the second cycle of the United Nations Convention against Corruption (UNCAC) implementation review mechanism.
Working alongside representatives from Tanzania and the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), the Djiboutian experts contributed to the assessment of Madagascar's legal and institutional framework for preventing corruption and recovering illicit assets.
The review examined the country's compliance with the preventive measures outlined in Chapter II of the Convention and the asset recovery provisions contained in Chapter V. During the mission, the delegation met senior Malagasy officials, including the Prime Minister, parliamentary leaders, and representatives of the Ministries of Justice and Foreign Affairs, to discuss national anti-corruption policies and institutional reforms.
Djibouti's participation in the international review process highlights its increasing role in promoting transparency and good governance across Africa. By contributing to the evaluation of partner countries while also participating in the Convention's mutual review mechanism, the country continues to support the strengthening of international standards for integrity and public accountability.
Together, the missions to Côte d'Ivoire and Madagascar underscore Djibouti's growing commitment to international cooperation as a key instrument in combating corruption. Through stronger partnerships, technical exchanges, and active participation in multilateral initiatives, the country aims to reinforce institutional capacity and promote governance systems that foster public trust and sustainable development.

title_en: Sudanese Army Retakes Strategic Border Town of Kurmuk in Blue Nile
excerpt_en: KURMUK, July 8, 2026 — The Sudanese army has regained control of the strategic border town of Kurmuk in the Blue Nile region after intense clashes with forces from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and a faction of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N) led by…
body_en:
KURMUK, July 8, 2026 — The Sudanese army has regained control of the strategic border town of Kurmuk in the Blue Nile region after intense clashes with forces from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and a faction of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N) led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu.
The army’s advance ends months of control by the RSF and its allied fighters, who captured Kurmuk on March 24 during a major military operation in the border area near Ethiopia.
Sudanese authorities had previously accused Ethiopia of supporting the assault by allowing drone operations from Bahir Dar airport in the Amhara region. Ethiopian officials rejected the allegations.
The recapture was confirmed by Brigadier General Abadi al-Tahir, commander of the army’s Al-Naba al-Yaqeen task force, who said government forces had inflicted significant losses on opposing fighters and equipment, forcing surviving forces to withdraw.
The operation followed weeks of military movements by the army to secure areas surrounding Kurmuk and push RSF forces away from the strategic location.
Located near Sudan’s border with Ethiopia, Kurmuk has historically been a key battlefield due to its strategic importance. The town has repeatedly changed control during Sudan’s long-running conflicts, including the decades-long civil war between Khartoum and the SPLM under the leadership of the late John Garang.
