title: Dangote Chooses Kenya Over Tanzania for Planned East African Oil Refinery
excerpt: NAIROBI, Kenya, July 8, 2026 - Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote has announced that his planned East African oil refinery will be built in Kenya instead of Tanzania, ending months of speculation over the location of the multibillion-dollar project. The refinery is expected…
title_en: Dangote Chooses Kenya Over Tanzania for Planned East African Oil Refinery
excerpt_en: NAIROBI, Kenya, July 8, 2026 - Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote has announced that his planned East African oil refinery will be built in Kenya instead of Tanzania, ending months of speculation over the location of the multibillion-dollar project. The refinery is expected…
body_en:
NAIROBI, Kenya, July 8, 2026 - Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote has announced that his planned East African oil refinery will be built in Kenya instead of Tanzania, ending months of speculation over the location of the multibillion-dollar project.
The refinery is expected to be constructed on Lamu Island and will have a processing capacity of 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day, making it the largest refinery in East Africa and among the biggest on the African continent. Construction is projected to take approximately 30 months.
Once completed, the facility is expected to supply refined petroleum products to Kenya and neighboring countries, strengthening regional energy security, reducing reliance on imported fuel, and supporting Kenya's ambition to become a regional petroleum trading hub. The project is also expected to generate thousands of jobs during construction and operation.
The decision follows discussions between Dangote and Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu Hassan, during which the businessman reportedly cited technical and commercial considerations for selecting Kenya. The project builds on Dangote's broader strategy to expand Africa's refining capacity following the launch of his refinery in Lagos, Nigeria.

title: Zimbabwe Enacts Constitutional Changes Extending President Mnangagwa's Time in Office
excerpt: HARARE, Zimbabwe, July 7, 2026 - Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa has signed into law a constitutional amendment introducing sweeping electoral reforms, including postponing the next general elections to 2030 and extending the terms of the president and parliament. The…
title_en: Zimbabwe Enacts Constitutional Changes Extending President Mnangagwa's Time in Office
excerpt_en: HARARE, Zimbabwe, July 7, 2026 - Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa has signed into law a constitutional amendment introducing sweeping electoral reforms, including postponing the next general elections to 2030 and extending the terms of the president and parliament. The…
body_en:
HARARE, Zimbabwe, July 7, 2026 - Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa has signed into law a constitutional amendment introducing sweeping electoral reforms, including postponing the next general elections to 2030 and extending the terms of the president and parliament.
The legislation, approved by Parliament in June, extends presidential and parliamentary terms from five to seven years and replaces direct presidential elections with a system in which the head of state is elected by members of Parliament. The changes also postpone elections that had been scheduled for 2028, allowing Mnangagwa to remain in office until 2030.
The reforms have drawn criticism from opposition parties, civil society organizations, human rights groups, and some veterans of Zimbabwe's liberation struggle, who argue that changes affecting the presidency should be approved through a national referendum. Supporters of the amendment contend that Parliament acted within its constitutional authority because the existing two-term presidential limit remains in place, with only the duration of each term being altered.
The constitutional changes come amid ongoing political debate in Zimbabwe, where several legal challenges have been filed seeking to overturn the reforms. Mnangagwa has served as president since 2017, following the removal of longtime leader Robert Mugabe from office.

title: Rwanda and Poland Celebrate Liberation Day and Six Decades of Diplomatic Relations
excerpt: WARSAW, Poland, July 7, 2026 - Rwanda marked the 32nd Liberation Day in Poland with celebrations highlighting more than six decades of diplomatic relations between the two countries and their growing cooperation in diplomacy, trade, and development. The ceremony, held in…
title_en: Rwanda and Poland Celebrate Liberation Day and Six Decades of Diplomatic Relations
excerpt_en: WARSAW, Poland, July 7, 2026 - Rwanda marked the 32nd Liberation Day in Poland with celebrations highlighting more than six decades of diplomatic relations between the two countries and their growing cooperation in diplomacy, trade, and development. The ceremony, held in…
body_en:
WARSAW, Poland, July 7, 2026 - Rwanda marked the 32nd Liberation Day in Poland with celebrations highlighting more than six decades of diplomatic relations between the two countries and their growing cooperation in diplomacy, trade, and development.
The ceremony, held in Warsaw, brought together Polish government officials, diplomats, academics, business representatives, members of the Rwandan community, and friends of Rwanda. Participants reflected on Rwanda's progress since the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi and the strengthening of bilateral ties, including the establishment of resident embassies and expanded economic cooperation.
Rwanda's Ambassador to Poland, Prof. Anastase Shyaka, paid tribute to the Rwanda Patriotic Front (RPF-Inkotanyi) and the former Rwanda Patriotic Army (RPA) for ending the genocide and laying the foundation for national unity, security, and development. He also thanked Polish institutions and partners for their support during his five-year tenure as ambassador, noting that his term had come to an end.
Representing the Polish government, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs Wojciech Zajączkowski praised Rwanda's recovery and resilience, describing the country's transformation as a remarkable achievement after the tragedy of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi. The event concluded with cultural performances by members of the Rwandan diaspora, celebrating the friendship between the two nations.

excerpt: KIGALI, Rwanda, July 7, 2026 - Rwanda is strengthening the quality of its agricultural exports through an internationally accredited laboratory operated by the National Agricultural Export Development Board (NAEB), which tests soil, fertilizers, irrigation water, and…
title_en: NAEB Laboratory Strengthens Quality Control for Rwanda's Agricultural Exports
excerpt_en: KIGALI, Rwanda, July 7, 2026 - Rwanda is strengthening the quality of its agricultural exports through an internationally accredited laboratory operated by the National Agricultural Export Development Board (NAEB), which tests soil, fertilizers, irrigation water, and…
body_en:
KIGALI, Rwanda, July 7, 2026 - Rwanda is strengthening the quality of its agricultural exports through an internationally accredited laboratory operated by the National Agricultural Export Development Board (NAEB), which tests soil, fertilizers, irrigation water, and agricultural products to ensure they meet global market standards.
The laboratory analyzes crops for pesticide residues, contaminants, mold, and other quality indicators before export, while also testing soil and water to help farmers improve productivity and select appropriate fertilizers. It additionally certifies the quality of products such as coffee, tea, and honey, reducing the risk of export rejections and financial losses for producers and exporters.
NAEB officials said the facility's recent international accreditation confirms that its testing procedures meet globally recognized standards. The laboratory is equipped with advanced technology and specialized personnel to support Rwanda's efforts to improve the competitiveness of its agricultural exports.
Authorities are encouraging farmers and exporters to routinely test their soil, water, and produce before cultivation and export, saying the practice will improve yields, ensure compliance with international regulations, and protect Rwanda's reputation in global markets. The initiative forms part of the country's broader strategy to increase export earnings and drive economic growth through higher-value agricultural production.

title: Sudan Partners with China Harbour to Modernize Port Infrastructure
excerpt: PORT SUDAN, July 7, 2026 - Sudan has signed a cooperation agreement with China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC) to upgrade port infrastructure, modernize equipment, and strengthen the country’s position as a regional trade hub. The memorandum of understanding was signed by…
title_en: Sudan Partners with China Harbour to Modernize Port Infrastructure
excerpt_en: PORT SUDAN, July 7, 2026 - Sudan has signed a cooperation agreement with China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC) to upgrade port infrastructure, modernize equipment, and strengthen the country’s position as a regional trade hub. The memorandum of understanding was signed by…
body_en:
PORT SUDAN, July 7, 2026 - Sudan has signed a cooperation agreement with China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC) to upgrade port infrastructure, modernize equipment, and strengthen the country’s position as a regional trade hub.
The memorandum of understanding was signed by the Sudanese Sea Ports Corporation (SPC) in Beijing, with the participation of Sudan’s Ambassador to China, Omer Issa. The agreement aims to address long-standing operational challenges at the Port of Port Sudan, which have affected its ability to accommodate large vessels and expand transshipment activities.
The planned projects include the modernization of port equipment, including gantry cranes, the improvement of digital and information systems, and the development of new seaport facilities.
Officials said the partnership is expected to increase operational efficiency, improve the competitiveness of Sudanese ports, and support economic growth by expanding transit trade opportunities.
The agreement follows recent improvements at Port Sudan’s Southern Port, where the container terminal received large container ships for the first time, a move authorities said strengthened confidence among international shipping operators.
However, Sudan’s main maritime gateway still requires major expansion, including deeper berths and increased capacity to meet the needs of modern global shipping. The port currently has nearly 1,478 metres of berthing space and storage areas covering around 1.48 million square metres, capacities considered limited compared with major international ports.
The government hopes the infrastructure partnership with China will help transform Port Sudan into a more competitive regional logistics centre and strengthen Sudan’s role in international trade.

title: Djibouti Hosts Regional Workshop to Strengthen Health Financing Oversight
excerpt: Djibouti City, July 7, 2026 - Djibouti has brought together financial oversight officials and public audit experts from nine French-speaking African countries for a regional workshop aimed at improving transparency and accountability in the management of international health…
title_en: Djibouti Hosts Regional Workshop to Strengthen Health Financing Oversight
excerpt_en: Djibouti City, July 7, 2026 - Djibouti has brought together financial oversight officials and public audit experts from nine French-speaking African countries for a regional workshop aimed at improving transparency and accountability in the management of international health…
body_en:
Djibouti City, July 7, 2026 - Djibouti has brought together financial oversight officials and public audit experts from nine French-speaking African countries for a regional workshop aimed at improving transparency and accountability in the management of international health funding.
The meeting, organized under the Project to Support the Monitoring of Subsidies Linked to Global Health Initiatives (PASSIMS), was hosted by the Djibouti Court of Auditors in collaboration with the Regional Training Council of Supreme Audit Institutions in French-speaking Sub-Saharan Africa (CREFIAF). The workshop focuses on strengthening financial governance and enhancing oversight of funds allocated to combat major diseases and reinforce national health systems.
Opening the event, the First President of Djibouti's Court of Auditors emphasized the importance of ensuring that international health financing is managed with the highest standards of accountability, transparency, and financial traceability. She noted that maintaining rigorous oversight is essential to preserving the confidence of development partners while improving public financial management.
Participants also highlighted the broader role of supreme audit institutions in promoting good governance, reinforcing institutional integrity, and supporting public authorities through independent oversight and advisory functions.
The workshop has brought together magistrates, auditors, and financial specialists from Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Madagascar, Mali, Senegal, Chad, and Djibouti to exchange experiences and strengthen regional cooperation in public financial auditing.
Discussions are centered on improving oversight of international funding dedicated to combating HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria, as well as expanding vaccination programs and strengthening health systems. The PASSIMS initiative supports more effective monitoring of grants provided by international health partners, helping ensure that financial resources are used efficiently and reach their intended beneficiaries.
The sessions build on previous technical meetings held both in person and virtually, while encouraging participating institutions to harmonize their audit practices using internationally recognized standards developed by the International Organization of Supreme Audit Institutions (INTOSAI).
Beyond technical training, the workshop seeks to foster a regional community of practice by encouraging collaboration, knowledge sharing, and the exchange of expertise among public auditors across French-speaking Africa. Organizers noted that transforming individual experience into collective expertise is essential for strengthening financial governance throughout the region.
For Djibouti, hosting the regional gathering reinforces its growing role as a center for cooperation on public financial management and governance issues in French-speaking Africa.
The initiative also underscores the broader importance of sound financial oversight in the health sector, recognizing that transparent management of public resources remains a key factor in strengthening health systems, improving service delivery, and ensuring better access to healthcare for populations across the continent.

title: Rwanda Says New Kenya and Tanzania Deals Will Strengthen Regional Fuel Trade
excerpt: KIGALI, Rwanda, July 7, 2026 - Rwanda expects recently signed petroleum cooperation agreements with Kenya and Tanzania to strengthen fuel supply security and position the country as a regional trading hub for petroleum products, Trade and Industry Minister Antoine Marie…
title_en: Rwanda Says New Kenya and Tanzania Deals Will Strengthen Regional Fuel Trade
excerpt_en: KIGALI, Rwanda, July 7, 2026 - Rwanda expects recently signed petroleum cooperation agreements with Kenya and Tanzania to strengthen fuel supply security and position the country as a regional trading hub for petroleum products, Trade and Industry Minister Antoine Marie…
body_en:
KIGALI, Rwanda, July 7, 2026 - Rwanda expects recently signed petroleum cooperation agreements with Kenya and Tanzania to strengthen fuel supply security and position the country as a regional trading hub for petroleum products, Trade and Industry Minister Antoine Marie Kajangwe has said.
The minister said the agreements will enable Rwanda to import petroleum products through the ports of Mombasa in Kenya and Tanga in Tanzania under government-backed arrangements designed to improve storage, transportation, and supply chain efficiency.
The agreement with Kenya, signed on June 29, establishes a government-to-government framework for importing fuel through the Port of Mombasa, providing Rwanda with access to storage facilities, pipeline infrastructure, and transport services. A separate agreement with Tanzania allows the importation of petrol and diesel through the Port of Tanga under a partnership involving the Rwanda National Energy Corporation (RNEC) and Gulf Bulk Petroleum Tanzania Limited.
Kajangwe said the new arrangements are expected to improve the reliability of Rwanda's fuel imports, reduce logistical bottlenecks, and create opportunities for the country to supply petroleum products to neighboring markets. The agreements come as Rwanda and other countries continue to face pressure from rising global fuel prices.
As a landlocked country, Rwanda relies entirely on overland imports of petroleum products, with the ports of Mombasa and Dar es Salaam serving as its principal gateways for fuel supplies.

title: Drone Attacks Kill 15 Civilians in North Kordofan as Sudan Conflict Intensifies
excerpt: HAMRAT AL-SHEIKH, July 7, 2026 - At least 15 civilians have been killed in two separate drone strikes targeting civilian vehicles in Sudan’s North Kordofan state, amid a growing wave of attacks that has caused widespread casualties and damage to essential infrastructure. The…
title_en: Drone Attacks Kill 15 Civilians in North Kordofan as Sudan Conflict Intensifies
excerpt_en: HAMRAT AL-SHEIKH, July 7, 2026 - At least 15 civilians have been killed in two separate drone strikes targeting civilian vehicles in Sudan’s North Kordofan state, amid a growing wave of attacks that has caused widespread casualties and damage to essential infrastructure. The…
body_en:
HAMRAT AL-SHEIKH, July 7, 2026 - At least 15 civilians have been killed in two separate drone strikes targeting civilian vehicles in Sudan’s North Kordofan state, amid a growing wave of attacks that has caused widespread casualties and damage to essential infrastructure.
The first strike occurred on Monday in Al-Shaatoot, east of Jabrat al-Sheikh locality, when a drone hit a vehicle carrying people travelling to a wedding. The attack killed 13 civilians, including five women.
A second strike took place on Tuesday morning in the Hamrat al-Sheikh area, where a drone targeted a civilian vehicle transporting water near a water source, killing two people.
The attacks are part of a broader escalation of drone operations in the Kordofan region, where civilians have increasingly been caught in the fighting between rival forces. Previous strikes have damaged schools, hospitals, and water facilities, further worsening humanitarian conditions.
Human rights advocates warned that repeated attacks on civilian movements and essential resources are creating fear among communities and restricting access to basic needs.
The legal group said the continued targeting of civilian areas raises concerns over possible violations of international humanitarian law and called for an independent investigation to identify those responsible.
It urged all parties involved in the conflict to immediately stop attacks against civilians, allow humanitarian access, and respect international rules protecting non-combatants during armed conflicts.

title: Ugandan Court Orders Inquest into 2018 Killing of Bobi Wine’s Driver
excerpt: Kampala, Uganda, July 7, 2026 - Uganda's High Court has ordered a formal judicial inquest into the 2018 killing of Yasin Kawuma, the driver of opposition leader Bobi Wine, reopening one of the country's most high-profile unresolved political cases nearly eight years after the…
title_en: Ugandan Court Orders Inquest into 2018 Killing of Bobi Wine’s Driver
excerpt_en: Kampala, Uganda, July 7, 2026 - Uganda's High Court has ordered a formal judicial inquest into the 2018 killing of Yasin Kawuma, the driver of opposition leader Bobi Wine, reopening one of the country's most high-profile unresolved political cases nearly eight years after the…
body_en:
Kampala, Uganda, July 7, 2026 - Uganda's High Court has ordered a formal judicial inquest into the 2018 killing of Yasin Kawuma, the driver of opposition leader Bobi Wine, reopening one of the country's most high-profile unresolved political cases nearly eight years after the fatal shooting.
The ruling directs the Chief Magistrate's Court in Arua to conduct a public fact-finding inquiry into the circumstances surrounding Kawuma's death, concluding that a judicial inquest is necessary to establish how the incident occurred and to serve the interests of justice, the victim's family, and the public.
The decision follows a legal application filed by Kawuma's widow, who sought judicial intervention after years without a criminal prosecution or official inquiry into the killing. While the court held that it could not compel the executive to appoint a coroner, it ruled that it had independent authority under the law to order an inquest.
Kawuma was fatally shot on August 13, 2018, during violence that erupted in Arua amid parliamentary by-election campaigns. He was seated inside a vehicle used by Bobi Wine when a bullet pierced the windscreen, killing him instantly. The incident occurred as security forces clashed with opposition supporters following unrest linked to campaign activities.
The killing triggered widespread public outrage and was followed by the arrest of Bobi Wine, several opposition lawmakers, and dozens of supporters, who were later charged with treason before the charges were eventually withdrawn.
The forthcoming inquest will examine the identity of the deceased and determine how, when, and where he died. As a judicial inquest, the proceedings are intended to establish the facts surrounding the death rather than determine criminal responsibility.

title: Burundi Consultations: C64 Coalition Returns to Kinshasa to Present Outcome of Ndayishimiye Dialogue Initiative
excerpt: Kinshasa, July 7, 2026 - The Article 64 Coalition for the Defense of Constitutional Order (C64) has announced a press conference in Kinshasa following consultations held in Bujumbura with Burundian President and African Union Chairperson Évariste Ndayishimiye on the political…
title_en: Burundi Consultations: C64 Coalition Returns to Kinshasa to Present Outcome of Ndayishimiye Dialogue Initiative
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, July 7, 2026 - The Article 64 Coalition for the Defense of Constitutional Order (C64) has announced a press conference in Kinshasa following consultations held in Bujumbura with Burundian President and African Union Chairperson Évariste Ndayishimiye on the political…
body_en:
Kinshasa, July 7, 2026 - The Article 64 Coalition for the Defense of Constitutional Order (C64) has announced a press conference in Kinshasa following consultations held in Bujumbura with Burundian President and African Union Chairperson Évariste Ndayishimiye on the political and institutional situation in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The discussions, held on July 6 in Burundi’s capital, brought together representatives of the Congolese opposition, major religious denominations, and President Ndayishimiye, who sought to encourage dialogue among Congolese stakeholders as a possible avenue for addressing the country’s political tensions.
According to participants, the consultations took place in a calm and constructive atmosphere. Separate meetings were first held with representatives of different religious groups, including leaders of Revival Churches, the Church of Christ in Congo (ECC), and the National Episcopal Conference of Congo (CENCO), before a broader session brought together all delegations and the Burundian authorities.
A representative of the C64 coalition described the discussions as positive, emphasizing that the exchanges focused on the need to find solutions through dialogue and political engagement.
Following their return to Kinshasa, the coalition and religious representatives plan to hold a press conference to present the main points emerging from the Bujumbura consultations.
The C64 delegation said Évariste Ndayishimiye, in his role as African Union chairperson, intends to contribute to efforts aimed at resolving the Congolese crisis by promoting dialogue between the various political actors.
The consultations took place amid growing tensions surrounding a proposed constitutional amendment in the DRC, which opponents argue could open the way for President Félix Tshisekedi to seek another term in office.
The C64 coalition had initially planned a nationwide demonstration on July 8 to protest against the constitutional reform initiative. However, the movement was postponed to July 22, 2026, following the invitation from President Ndayishimiye for political consultations.
The coalition, which includes several opposition figures such as Martin Fayulu, Delly Sesanga, Moïse Katumbi, and Jean-Marc Kabund, said it accepted the invitation in a spirit of responsibility, while maintaining its concerns regarding constitutional order, democratic stability, and institutional balance.
During his recent visit to Kinshasa, Évariste Ndayishimiye had already called on Congolese political actors to prioritize dialogue, preserve national unity, and strengthen institutional stability amid continuing security challenges, particularly in eastern DRC.
Through these consultations, the Burundian president seeks to position dialogue and consensus-building as key elements in addressing the political challenges facing the Democratic Republic of Congo.

title: JEEMA Sets Ambitious Target for Local Council Elections, Calls for Political Change from Grassroots
excerpt: Kampala, Uganda, July 7, 2026 - The Justice Forum (JEEMA) has announced plans to win at least 65 per cent of Local Council I (LC1) and Local Council II (LC2) positions in Uganda’s upcoming grassroots elections, describing the polls as a key opportunity to drive political…
title_en: JEEMA Sets Ambitious Target for Local Council Elections, Calls for Political Change from Grassroots
excerpt_en: Kampala, Uganda, July 7, 2026 - The Justice Forum (JEEMA) has announced plans to win at least 65 per cent of Local Council I (LC1) and Local Council II (LC2) positions in Uganda’s upcoming grassroots elections, describing the polls as a key opportunity to drive political…
body_en:
Kampala, Uganda, July 7, 2026 - The Justice Forum (JEEMA) has announced plans to win at least 65 per cent of Local Council I (LC1) and Local Council II (LC2) positions in Uganda’s upcoming grassroots elections, describing the polls as a key opportunity to drive political change from village-level leadership.
The opposition party said it aims to secure victories in approximately 46,000 of Uganda’s 71,227 villages, arguing that control of local councils would strengthen citizen participation in governance and influence the country’s political direction.
JEEMA accused the ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) of dominating Uganda’s political and economic affairs for nearly four decades and urged voters to use the grassroots elections as an opportunity to support alternative leadership.
The party’s spokesperson said village councils are central to local governance, playing important roles in areas such as land management, community security, healthcare access, and development planning.
JEEMA also criticized rising public debt, resource management, and economic challenges affecting citizens, warning that current policies could create greater burdens for future generations.
The party urged voters to reject vote buying, arguing that exchanging votes for short-term benefits undermines accountability and slows national development. It called on citizens to view their votes as a tool for demanding better leadership and public service delivery.
JEEMA pledged to field candidates across all 71,227 villages and 10,595 parishes, either independently or in partnership with other democratic groups. Although acknowledging financial limitations, the party said it would support candidates through training, campaign guidance, and policy materials.
The Electoral Commission has begun preparations for the long-delayed LC1 and LC2 elections, which are expected to restore elected grassroots leadership structures after years without fresh polls.
The elections are considered a significant step in strengthening local governance ahead of Uganda’s next national electoral cycle.

title: DRC Uses UN Security Council Presidency to Push Global Action Against Conflict-Related Sexual Violence
excerpt: New York, July 7, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo is preparing to use its presidency of the United Nations Security Council to place the protection of civilians, the fight against impunity, and the Women, Peace and Security agenda at the center of international…
title_en: DRC Uses UN Security Council Presidency to Push Global Action Against Conflict-Related Sexual Violence
excerpt_en: New York, July 7, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo is preparing to use its presidency of the United Nations Security Council to place the protection of civilians, the fight against impunity, and the Women, Peace and Security agenda at the center of international…
body_en:
New York, July 7, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo is preparing to use its presidency of the United Nations Security Council to place the protection of civilians, the fight against impunity, and the Women, Peace and Security agenda at the center of international discussions.
For the first time in more than three decades, Kinshasa is holding the rotating presidency of the Security Council, which began on July 1, 2026. The government intends to use this diplomatic platform to highlight issues drawn from its own experience with prolonged conflict, particularly in eastern DRC.
As part of this agenda, Prime Minister Judith Suminwa will chair a high-level public debate in New York on July 8 under the theme: “Women, Peace and Security - Honoring the Promise of International Law to Survivors of Conflict-Related Sexual Violence.”
The meeting comes amid renewed concerns over conflict-related sexual violence in several regions worldwide, including eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, where civilians continue to face serious security challenges.
According to the Congolese government, the debate aims to give greater visibility to survivors and encourage the international community to transform existing commitments into concrete measures. Discussions are expected to focus on strengthening accountability mechanisms, improving access to healthcare and justice for victims, expanding reparations programs, and ensuring long-term reintegration support.
Kinshasa also intends to highlight the links between sexual violence, conflict economies, and the illegal exploitation of natural resources, arguing that these factors contribute to the continuation of instability in conflict-affected areas.
The debate will mark the beginning of a broader diplomatic initiative focused on peace, security, and natural resource governance. A meeting under the Arria formula is scheduled for July 13 to examine the relationship between natural resources and conflict, followed by a high-level debate on July 21 dedicated to “Natural Resource Governance: The Foundation of Peace, Security, and Prosperity.”
Through its Security Council presidency, the DRC says it aims to contribute its experience to global discussions on peacebuilding, justice, and civilian protection while advocating for stronger international responses to crises.
The country joined the United Nations Security Council as one of five new non-permanent members for the 2026-2027 term, alongside Bahrain, Colombia, Latvia, and Liberia. Although elected members do not hold veto power, they participate fully in negotiations and voting processes and can influence the Council’s agenda and resolutions.
During its mandate, the DRC is also part of the A3 group, which brings together African countries serving on the Security Council. This framework allows coordination with other African members and contributes to the representation of African Union positions on issues affecting the continent.

title: FARDC and Wazalendo Repel AFC/M23 Attack Near Strategic Mindjendje Position
excerpt: Walikale, July 7, 2026 - A fragile calm has returned to Mindjendje, in the Banakindi area of the Kisimba group, Walikale territory, following clashes between AFC/M23 fighters and government forces supported by Wazalendo armed groups. The fighting broke out on Monday, July 6,…
title_en: FARDC and Wazalendo Repel AFC/M23 Attack Near Strategic Mindjendje Position
excerpt_en: Walikale, July 7, 2026 - A fragile calm has returned to Mindjendje, in the Banakindi area of the Kisimba group, Walikale territory, following clashes between AFC/M23 fighters and government forces supported by Wazalendo armed groups. The fighting broke out on Monday, July 6,…
body_en:
Walikale, July 7, 2026 - A fragile calm has returned to Mindjendje, in the Banakindi area of the Kisimba group, Walikale territory, following clashes between AFC/M23 fighters and government forces supported by Wazalendo armed groups.
The fighting broke out on Monday, July 6, when AFC/M23 elements launched an offensive against positions held by the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and their allies. According to local sources, the attackers advanced from Malemo, located in the Bashali Mokoto group of Masisi territory, with the objective of taking control of the strategic Mindjendje area.
The confrontation lasted several hours, with heavy and light weapons fire reported across the area. The intensity of the clashes caused panic among residents of nearby villages, particularly Mpety and Nzanganano, where communities feared the violence could spread further.
According to local sources, FARDC troops, supported by Wazalendo fighters, managed to halt the offensive and push back the attackers. AFC/M23 forces reportedly withdrew toward Malemo, their initial position.
No official information has been released regarding casualties or material damage resulting from the clashes. However, local authorities indicate that Mindjendje remains under the control of government forces and their allies.
The latest fighting highlights the continued instability along the border areas between Walikale and Masisi territories, where repeated confrontations between armed groups and security forces continue to threaten civilians and worsen humanitarian concerns in North Kivu.

excerpt: Bukavu, July 7, 2026 - Fighting has intensified in the highlands of Fizi, Mwenga, and Uvira territories in South Kivu province, where the Congolese army, supported by Wazalendo fighters, has launched operations aimed at regaining positions taken by AFC/M23 forces. The…
title_en: FARDC Launches Offensive Against AFC/M23 Positions in Fizi, Mwenga and Uvira Highlands
excerpt_en: Bukavu, July 7, 2026 - Fighting has intensified in the highlands of Fizi, Mwenga, and Uvira territories in South Kivu province, where the Congolese army, supported by Wazalendo fighters, has launched operations aimed at regaining positions taken by AFC/M23 forces. The…
body_en:
Bukavu, July 7, 2026 - Fighting has intensified in the highlands of Fizi, Mwenga, and Uvira territories in South Kivu province, where the Congolese army, supported by Wazalendo fighters, has launched operations aimed at regaining positions taken by AFC/M23 forces.
The clashes, which began on July 1, have affected several villages in the highland areas, a remote region where limited communication networks have made it difficult to obtain immediate and independent information from the ground.
According to military authorities, AFC/M23 elements, operating alongside allied armed groups, had recently seized several strategic positions around Minembwe, including Point Zero and Rugezi.
In response, the FARDC announced the launch of a counteroffensive to recover territories lost during the previous fighting. Lieutenant Reagan Mbuyi Kalonji, spokesperson for Operation Sukola 2 South Kivu, said government forces had regained control of key positions, including Kimete, Wihene, and Kashamata.
The military spokesperson added that AFC/M23-Twirwaneho-RDF-Red Tabara coalition elements had been forced to withdraw toward Rugezi and Bigaragara, areas located south of Minembwe.
The fighting has also raised concerns over civilian casualties. The FARDC reported that AFC/M23 drones allegedly targeted populated areas, including Bidjaga village east of Point Zero, causing around ten deaths according to military statements.
The situation remains uncertain in the highlands of South Kivu, where competing armed groups continue to fight for control of strategic locations. The renewed clashes are further increasing security risks for communities already affected by years of instability and displacement.

title: Minister Urges Former Armed Group Members to Rebuild Their Lives After Returning to Rwanda
excerpt: MUSANZE, Rwanda, July 7, 2026 - Rwanda's Minister of Gender and Family Development, Consolée Uwimana, has encouraged former members of armed groups operating in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo to embrace their return home as an opportunity to rebuild their lives and…
title_en: Minister Urges Former Armed Group Members to Rebuild Their Lives After Returning to Rwanda
excerpt_en: MUSANZE, Rwanda, July 7, 2026 - Rwanda's Minister of Gender and Family Development, Consolée Uwimana, has encouraged former members of armed groups operating in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo to embrace their return home as an opportunity to rebuild their lives and…
body_en:
MUSANZE, Rwanda, July 7, 2026 - Rwanda's Minister of Gender and Family Development, Consolée Uwimana, has encouraged former members of armed groups operating in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo to embrace their return home as an opportunity to rebuild their lives and contribute to the country's development.
Speaking at the inauguration of an Early Childhood Development (ECD) center at the Mutobo Reintegration Centre, the minister said the return of former combatants, including ex-members of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), marks the beginning of a new chapter focused on reconciliation, rehabilitation, and national development. The new facility will provide services for the children of former combatants undergoing reintegration.
Uwimana said Rwanda's progress over the past three decades has been driven by unity, accountability, and a shared commitment to national development. She urged the returnees to use the vocational skills and support provided through the reintegration program to build stable families, pursue lawful livelihoods, and contribute positively to their communities.
According to the Rwanda Demobilization and Reintegration Commission (RDRC), more than 12,600 former members of armed groups operating in eastern DR Congo have been rehabilitated and reintegrated into society since 2001.

title: UN Demands Humanitarian Access in Sudan as Civilian and Child Casualties Rise
excerpt: UNITED NATIONS, July 7, 2026 - The United Nations has called for greater humanitarian access in Sudan as fighting intensifies across several regions, with growing concerns over civilian casualties, drone attacks, and restrictions affecting aid operations. The UN humanitarian…
title_en: UN Demands Humanitarian Access in Sudan as Civilian and Child Casualties Rise
excerpt_en: UNITED NATIONS, July 7, 2026 - The United Nations has called for greater humanitarian access in Sudan as fighting intensifies across several regions, with growing concerns over civilian casualties, drone attacks, and restrictions affecting aid operations. The UN humanitarian…
body_en:
UNITED NATIONS, July 7, 2026 - The United Nations has called for greater humanitarian access in Sudan as fighting intensifies across several regions, with growing concerns over civilian casualties, drone attacks, and restrictions affecting aid operations.
The UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher held talks with Rapid Support Forces (RSF) leader General Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, urging the group to ensure safe access for humanitarian workers and civilians affected by the conflict.
Discussions focused on the worsening situation in areas such as El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, where violence and attacks on civilian infrastructure have disrupted relief efforts. The UN raised concerns over administrative obstacles preventing aid organizations from delivering assistance to vulnerable populations.
The call came as the UN Human Rights Council approved an urgent international investigation into alleged human rights violations and abuses in and around El Obeid. The inquiry will examine reported violations as fighting continues in the region.
The humanitarian situation has severely affected children, with UN figures indicating that at least 18 children have been killed and 17 injured in El Obeid since May. Across Sudan, more than 330 children were reportedly killed or injured during the first six months of 2026.
Despite ongoing insecurity, some humanitarian assistance has reached affected communities. A joint UN convoy carrying food and medical supplies arrived in Kadugli and Dilling in South Kordofan, providing support amid a growing cholera outbreak. The delivery marked the first UN aid shipment to reach the areas since early June.
In West Kordofan, where more than 800 cholera cases have been recorded, humanitarian agencies have allocated additional funding for water, sanitation, and emergency medical responses.
However, aid operations remain severely limited in parts of Darfur. Continued clashes in Kulbus locality in West Darfur have forced humanitarian organizations to suspend activities, while insecurity in Um Baru locality in North Darfur displaced more than 3,500 people in early July.
The UN continues to warn that the prolonged conflict is deepening Sudan’s humanitarian crisis, leaving millions of civilians in urgent need of protection and assistance.

title: Government Strengthens Coordination Between Regional Integration Ministry and P-DDRCS to Advance Peace Efforts
excerpt: Kinshasa, July 7, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has taken a new step toward improving coordination of peace and stabilization efforts with the signing of a cooperation agreement between the Ministry of Regional Integration and the Disarmament, Demobilization,…
title_en: Government Strengthens Coordination Between Regional Integration Ministry and P-DDRCS to Advance Peace Efforts
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, July 7, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has taken a new step toward improving coordination of peace and stabilization efforts with the signing of a cooperation agreement between the Ministry of Regional Integration and the Disarmament, Demobilization,…
body_en:
Kinshasa, July 7, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has taken a new step toward improving coordination of peace and stabilization efforts with the signing of a cooperation agreement between the Ministry of Regional Integration and the Disarmament, Demobilization, Community Recovery, and Stabilization Program (P-DDRCS).
The memorandum of understanding was signed on Monday, July 6, by Floribert Anzuluni, Minister of Regional Integration, and Jean de Dieu Désiré Ntanga Ntita, coordinator of the P-DDRCS. The agreement aims to strengthen collaboration between the two institutions in addressing cross-border conflicts and supporting peace initiatives in conflict-affected areas.
The partnership seeks to better connect national disarmament and reintegration mechanisms with regional peace frameworks. It will focus on coordinating stabilization programs, monitoring regional commitments related to peace and voluntary repatriation of foreign combatants, sharing strategic analysis on security dynamics, and mobilizing support from regional organizations and international partners.
Minister Floribert Anzuluni said the agreement responds to the urgent need for coordinated action to restore peace and security in eastern DRC, where armed conflicts involving local and foreign groups continue to affect communities.
He emphasized that although the P-DDRCS is primarily a national program, its mission also has a regional dimension due to the influence of cross-border armed groups and external factors contributing to insecurity.
The minister highlighted the importance of addressing the presence of foreign armed groups operating in the country, including the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), National Forces for the Liberation of Burundi (FNL), and Red Tabara. According to him, stronger cooperation between institutions is necessary to support voluntary disarmament and peaceful reintegration efforts.
Under the agreement, a Steering Committee will be established to provide strategic direction, while a Joint Technical Committee will oversee operational coordination, monitor activities, and evaluate progress.
For the P-DDRCS, the partnership represents an opportunity to strengthen the regional dimension of its strategy, particularly regarding disarmament, community recovery, stabilization, and the voluntary return of foreign combatants and their families.
Jean de Dieu Désiré Ntanga Ntita said the DRC’s decades-long experience with conflict has generated valuable expertise in peacebuilding, mediation, reintegration, and community stabilization. He argued that these lessons should be transformed into a structured national approach that could contribute to regional peace efforts.
The two institutions reaffirmed their commitment to protecting civilians, respecting human rights, strengthening state authority, and promoting transparency and accountability in peace initiatives.
The agreement is also expected to be presented within regional mechanisms, including the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR), with the objective of promoting greater coordination among neighboring countries facing similar security challenges.
The initiative comes as eastern DRC continues to face persistent insecurity linked to the activities of numerous armed groups. The ongoing violence has contributed to a growing humanitarian crisis, with increasing numbers of displaced populations and refugees seeking safety inside and outside the country.

title: Goma Showcases Resilience of Congolese Coffee and Cocoa Producers Despite Security Challenges
excerpt: Goma, North Kivu, July 7, 2026 - Coffee and cocoa producers from North and South Kivu are highlighting the potential of Congolese agriculture at the third edition of Best of Congo Cooperatives, an initiative aimed at promoting high-quality local products and attracting…
title_en: Goma Showcases Resilience of Congolese Coffee and Cocoa Producers Despite Security Challenges
excerpt_en: Goma, North Kivu, July 7, 2026 - Coffee and cocoa producers from North and South Kivu are highlighting the potential of Congolese agriculture at the third edition of Best of Congo Cooperatives, an initiative aimed at promoting high-quality local products and attracting…
body_en:
Goma, North Kivu, July 7, 2026 - Coffee and cocoa producers from North and South Kivu are highlighting the potential of Congolese agriculture at the third edition of Best of Congo Cooperatives, an initiative aimed at promoting high-quality local products and attracting international investment despite persistent insecurity in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Launched on July 2 in Goma by Congo Agri Platform in partnership with African Coffee Connect, the program brings together agricultural cooperatives working to strengthen the visibility and competitiveness of Congolese coffee and cocoa on global markets.
This year's edition features 34 Arabica coffee micro-lots from cooperatives in North and South Kivu, prepared for direct international auction. For the first time, the initiative also includes cocoa, with 34 lots representing different processing methods, including fully washed, natural, and anaerobic fermentation techniques.
Held under the theme “Business Climate: Promoting Investment,” the event aims to position coffee and cocoa as strategic sectors for economic growth while encouraging investment in agricultural value chains.
Agriculture Under Pressure from Insecurity
The gathering takes place in a difficult environment for producers in eastern DRC, where armed conflicts, limited infrastructure, and unreliable electricity continue to affect agricultural activities.
Despite these challenges, cooperatives from several territories continue producing crops mainly destined for international markets. Around twenty cooperatives from North and South Kivu participated in the event, representing producers from areas including Kabare, Kalehe, Idjwi, Masisi, Rutshuru, Beni, Lubero, as well as the cities of Beni and Butembo.
For farmers, insecurity remains one of the greatest obstacles to expanding production.
Bisimwa Lusari Leaandre, a coffee producer from Bushumba in Kabare Territory, explained that insecurity has reduced access to farmland and affected harvests. He called for stronger security measures to allow farmers to return safely to their fields and maintain production levels.
Infrastructure and Financing Challenges
Beyond security concerns, sector representatives highlighted structural challenges limiting the growth of coffee and cocoa industries.
Emmanuel Ntirata Ntale, African Coffee Connect's country representative, emphasized that Congolese Arabica coffee from the Kivu highlands enjoys international recognition, while cocoa production is also showing strong potential. However, he noted that poor road networks, limited electricity access, and difficulties obtaining financing continue to slow sector development.
He also stressed the need for agricultural policies capable of attracting long-term investors and creating a more stable business environment.
Building International Market Access
Ghislain Kamondo, Executive Director of Congo Agri Platform, said that insecurity has also affected certification processes, with some international inspection companies unable to operate in certain areas due to security restrictions.
Nevertheless, he highlighted the resilience of producers, noting increased participation in the program and growing interest in cocoa development.
Congo Agri Platform, which brings together more than 34 agricultural cooperatives, plays a key role in organizing supply chains, improving product quality, and connecting producers with international buyers.
Through the Best of Congo Cooperatives initiative, coffee and cocoa production is supported through traceability systems, including GPS-based tracking and geolocation of farms, helping producers meet international market standards.
Toward More Inclusive Agricultural Growth
The 2026 edition places particular emphasis on sustainable value chains and the participation of women, young people, and indigenous communities in agricultural development.
Despite insecurity and economic constraints, producers and cooperatives are seeking to demonstrate that eastern DRC's agricultural sector remains capable of competing internationally, provided that security, infrastructure, and investment challenges are addressed.

title: President Kagame Named Chair of UN Global Commission on Artificial Intelligence
excerpt: KIGALI, Rwanda, July 7, 2026 — Rwandan President Paul Kagame has been appointed chair of the newly established United Nations AI for Good Global Commission, a high-level body tasked with promoting the responsible and inclusive development of artificial intelligence worldwide.…
title_en: President Kagame Named Chair of UN Global Commission on Artificial Intelligence
excerpt_en: KIGALI, Rwanda, July 7, 2026 — Rwandan President Paul Kagame has been appointed chair of the newly established United Nations AI for Good Global Commission, a high-level body tasked with promoting the responsible and inclusive development of artificial intelligence worldwide.…
body_en:
KIGALI, Rwanda, July 7, 2026 — Rwandan President Paul Kagame has been appointed chair of the newly established United Nations AI for Good Global Commission, a high-level body tasked with promoting the responsible and inclusive development of artificial intelligence worldwide.
Kagame will lead the commission alongside Salesforce Chief Executive Marc Benioff, while International Telecommunication Union (ITU) Secretary-General Doreen Bogdan-Martin will serve as deputy chair. Supported by the ITU and UNESCO, the commission aims to reduce global technological disparities, promote international cooperation on AI, and help countries build capacity to harness emerging technologies.
The commission brings together more than 40 leaders from governments, international organizations, academia, and the technology industry, including executives from major global technology companies. Rather than developing binding regulations, it will focus on shaping global dialogue, promoting technical standards, and supporting AI adoption, particularly in developing countries.
Kagame's appointment reflects Rwanda's growing profile in digital innovation and technology policy. The country has expanded the use of artificial intelligence across sectors including healthcare, education, agriculture, justice, trade, and public services, while recently approving the creation of a national artificial intelligence agency to accelerate innovation, investment, and digital governance.

title: Sudan Turns to Alternative Economic Alliances Amid Pressure from Western Sanctions
excerpt: KHARTOUM, July 6, 2026 - Sudan’s government has adopted new economic strategies aimed at reducing the impact of Western sanctions and limiting the country’s dependence on traditional financial and trade partners, as the conflict with the Rapid Support Forces continues without…
title_en: Sudan Turns to Alternative Economic Alliances Amid Pressure from Western Sanctions
excerpt_en: KHARTOUM, July 6, 2026 - Sudan’s government has adopted new economic strategies aimed at reducing the impact of Western sanctions and limiting the country’s dependence on traditional financial and trade partners, as the conflict with the Rapid Support Forces continues without…
body_en:
KHARTOUM, July 6, 2026 - Sudan’s government has adopted new economic strategies aimed at reducing the impact of Western sanctions and limiting the country’s dependence on traditional financial and trade partners, as the conflict with the Rapid Support Forces continues without a clear path toward a negotiated settlement.
The new approach includes exploring alternative banking channels, promoting the use of local currencies in international trade, and strengthening ties with emerging economic blocs such as BRICS, according to government sources.
Authorities are seeking to diversify trade partnerships and reduce reliance on Western financial systems and major currencies, particularly the US dollar, as concerns grow over possible expansion of sanctions targeting individuals and entities linked to the Sudanese military.
Economists warn, however, that Sudan’s economic challenges go beyond sanctions. The country is facing a deep financial crisis caused by war, institutional fragmentation, declining exports, and disruptions to key sectors.
Economic experts said Sudan missed a major opportunity to reduce its debt burden after political instability following the 2021 military coup disrupted international financial cooperation and halted progress toward debt relief programs.
The war has severely affected Sudan’s banking system, with international financial institutions becoming increasingly cautious about dealing with the country. At the same time, disruptions to exports of key commodities such as gold, gum arabic, and oilseeds have reduced foreign currency revenues.
The continued depreciation of the Sudanese pound reflects broader economic problems linked to divided state institutions and competing authorities, which have created conflicting fiscal policies, increased taxation pressures, and weakened citizens’ purchasing power.
Sudan and China recently signed an agreement to reduce part of Beijing’s nearly $50 million debt and provide additional financial and technical support for reconstruction projects.
Meanwhile, international assessments indicate that the war has caused major economic losses, reversing decades of development progress, damaging social services, and weakening agricultural programs, leaving Sudan increasingly dependent on humanitarian assistance.

title: El Obeid Water Crisis Deepens as War Disrupts Supply Networks
excerpt: EL OBEID, July 6, 2026 - A severe water crisis is worsening in El Obeid as prolonged fighting, drone strikes, and power outages disrupt the city's main water supply systems, leaving millions of residents struggling to access clean drinking water. The capital of North Kordofan…
title_en: El Obeid Water Crisis Deepens as War Disrupts Supply Networks
excerpt_en: EL OBEID, July 6, 2026 - A severe water crisis is worsening in El Obeid as prolonged fighting, drone strikes, and power outages disrupt the city's main water supply systems, leaving millions of residents struggling to access clean drinking water. The capital of North Kordofan…
body_en:
EL OBEID, July 6, 2026 - A severe water crisis is worsening in El Obeid as prolonged fighting, drone strikes, and power outages disrupt the city's main water supply systems, leaving millions of residents struggling to access clean drinking water.
The capital of North Kordofan State has faced months of siege-like conditions, with recent attacks on critical infrastructure damaging electricity facilities and forcing the shutdown of major municipal water stations. The loss of power has affected the operation of water pumps, cutting off many neighborhoods from regular water supplies.
The city's two main water sources have been severely affected. The Al-Sidr basin to the south has been repeatedly targeted in attacks against utility infrastructure, while the Bara basin to the north remains inaccessible due to security conditions.
The water shortage comes as El Obeid experiences significant population pressure. The city's population has increased dramatically due to the arrival of large numbers of displaced people fleeing violence in other parts of Sudan, with many families now living in overcrowded camps or hosted by local communities.
Residents say the price of drinking water has sharply increased in recent weeks, forcing vulnerable households to either depend on expensive water deliveries or turn to unsafe sources. The situation has placed additional pressure on families already facing food shortages and rising living costs.
To respond to the emergency, local authorities and humanitarian partners have launched emergency water distribution efforts, deploying mobile water tankers to affected areas and supporting communities with limited access to essential supplies.
Authorities have also started a plan to expand alternative water sources, including drilling dozens of new wells, rehabilitating existing wells, and installing additional emergency water systems. Several new wells have already been completed as part of efforts to reduce dependence on damaged infrastructure.
Humanitarian groups warn that continued shortages of clean water, combined with fuel constraints and disrupted supply routes, could trigger a major public health emergency. The risk of waterborne diseases is increasing as thousands of residents remain trapped in difficult conditions amid the ongoing conflict.

title: Sudan Gold Mine Collapse Leaves 15 Miners Dead in Northern State
excerpt: WADI HALFA, July 6, 2026 - Fifteen gold miners were killed and another injured after a mine collapsed in Sudan’s Northern State, marking the latest in a series of deadly accidents affecting the country’s artisanal mining sector. The collapse occurred at the Mohamed Towfik…
title_en: Sudan Gold Mine Collapse Leaves 15 Miners Dead in Northern State
excerpt_en: WADI HALFA, July 6, 2026 - Fifteen gold miners were killed and another injured after a mine collapsed in Sudan’s Northern State, marking the latest in a series of deadly accidents affecting the country’s artisanal mining sector. The collapse occurred at the Mohamed Towfik…
body_en:
WADI HALFA, July 6, 2026 - Fifteen gold miners were killed and another injured after a mine collapsed in Sudan’s Northern State, marking the latest in a series of deadly accidents affecting the country’s artisanal mining sector.
The collapse occurred at the Mohamed Towfik gold mine in the Samna area of Wadi Halfa locality, where emergency teams were deployed to recover victims and assist with rescue operations.
Authorities said the operation involved coordination between mineral security forces, mining police, rescue teams, and local government officials. A technical team was also sent to investigate the circumstances surrounding the accident and assess safety conditions at the site.
Initial findings indicated that the miners entered the mine despite an earlier closure order issued by the Environment and Safety Department after technical inspections identified risks of collapse. Authorities said the decision to close the site had been taken to protect workers’ lives, but some miners reportedly ignored the warnings.
The latest incident adds to a growing number of deadly mining accidents across Sudan, including a similar collapse in Red Sea State earlier this year that killed several artisanal miners.
Sudan’s artisanal gold mining sector employs more than two million people, a figure that has increased since the outbreak of war in April 2023. The sector contributes more than 80% of the country’s gold production, with many miners operating in remote areas under dangerous working conditions.
Authorities have repeatedly announced plans to reorganize traditional mining activities, improve safety standards, and prevent unauthorized operations in high-risk areas to protect miners from further tragedies.

title: DRC Enacts Local Content Law to Increase Congolese Participation in Natural Resource Economy
excerpt: Kinshasa, July 6, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has taken a major step toward strengthening local participation in its economy with the enactment of a Local Content Law aimed at ensuring that the country's natural resources generate greater benefits for Congolese…
title_en: DRC Enacts Local Content Law to Increase Congolese Participation in Natural Resource Economy
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, July 6, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has taken a major step toward strengthening local participation in its economy with the enactment of a Local Content Law aimed at ensuring that the country's natural resources generate greater benefits for Congolese…
body_en:
Kinshasa, July 6, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has taken a major step toward strengthening local participation in its economy with the enactment of a Local Content Law aimed at ensuring that the country's natural resources generate greater benefits for Congolese businesses and communities.
The reform seeks to increase the involvement of local companies in industrial value chains, promote national expertise, and maximize the economic impact of the country's mineral wealth. It is being presented as a key milestone in efforts to transform natural resources into a stronger engine for inclusive development.
The law builds on a reform process launched under the leadership of Louis Watum Kabamba during his tenure as Minister of Industry and SME Development. In August 2024, a ministerial decree established a joint government-private sector commission tasked with reviewing the existing legal framework on private sector subcontracting and preparing proposals for a comprehensive local content policy.
The initiative aimed to modernize regulations initially established under the 2017 subcontracting law by creating stronger mechanisms for the participation of Congolese companies, entrepreneurs, and professionals in major economic sectors.
Following months of technical consultations and discussions with stakeholders, draft legislation was presented and later approved by the Council of Ministers in June 2025 before being submitted to Parliament for examination and adoption.
The promulgation of the Local Content Law now provides a formal framework for implementing these reforms, with several strategic objectives:
Supporting the growth of Congolese small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs);
Strengthening national subcontracting capacity;
Encouraging skills and technology transfer;
Positioning local content as a driver of economic development.
Authorities view the reform as part of a broader strategy to ensure that economic activities linked to mining, industry, and natural resources create more opportunities for Congolese citizens and contribute to long-term national development.
By establishing clearer rules for local participation, the government aims to move beyond resource extraction alone and encourage the development of domestic expertise, entrepreneurship, and industrial capacity across the country.

title: Nigeria Accuses South African Police Over Death of Citizen, Calls for Investigation

title_en: Nigeria Accuses South African Police Over Death of Citizen, Calls for Investigation
excerpt_en: ABUJA, Nigeria, July 6, 2026 - Nigeria has accused South African police of responsibility for the death of one of its citizens and called for stronger action to protect foreign nationals amid rising tensions and reported attacks on migrants in South Africa. Nigeria's Ministry…
body_en:
ABUJA, Nigeria, July 6, 2026 - Nigeria has accused South African police of responsibility for the death of one of its citizens and called for stronger action to protect foreign nationals amid rising tensions and reported attacks on migrants in South Africa.
Nigeria's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Emeka Charles Iroegbu died on June 28 in Pretoria after allegedly being subjected to excessive force while in police custody. The ministry also reported that another Nigerian national, businessman Musa Yunana Joe, was fatally shot by unidentified gunmen outside his shop in eMalahleni on the same day.
The Nigerian government said the incidents occurred against a backdrop of increasing hostility toward foreign nationals in South Africa and urged the South African authorities to conduct thorough investigations and strengthen measures to curb violence targeting migrants. It warned that the matter could be raised before the African Union and other international bodies if adequate action is not taken.
Nigeria also announced plans to support citizens who have returned from South Africa by documenting businesses and assets they left behind as part of a compensation initiative. South African authorities have not publicly commented on the reported deaths, while the government has maintained that it cannot provide compensation for affected foreign nationals but supports allowing them to dispose of their property through the local market.

title: Sudan War Leaves Hundreds of Children Dead or Injured as Violence Escalates
excerpt: KHARTOUM, July 6, 2026 - At least 330 children have been killed or injured across Sudan during the first half of 2026 as intensified fighting, drone strikes, and artillery attacks continue to devastate civilian areas, deepening the humanitarian crisis affecting the country’s…
title_en: Sudan War Leaves Hundreds of Children Dead or Injured as Violence Escalates
excerpt_en: KHARTOUM, July 6, 2026 - At least 330 children have been killed or injured across Sudan during the first half of 2026 as intensified fighting, drone strikes, and artillery attacks continue to devastate civilian areas, deepening the humanitarian crisis affecting the country’s…
body_en:
KHARTOUM, July 6, 2026 - At least 330 children have been killed or injured across Sudan during the first half of 2026 as intensified fighting, drone strikes, and artillery attacks continue to devastate civilian areas, deepening the humanitarian crisis affecting the country’s youngest population.
The worst impacts have been reported in Darfur and Kordofan, where ongoing clashes have exposed children to increasing risks from attacks on residential areas and essential infrastructure.
In North Kordofan, more than 35 children have reportedly been killed or injured since May alone, including 18 deaths. The victims included children between two months and 17 years old, with drone strikes accounting for a significant share of the reported casualties.
The growing use of drone warfare has transformed the nature of the conflict, with attacks increasingly reaching civilian neighborhoods, homes, markets, and public spaces where children and families seek safety.
Beyond the immediate loss of life, the war has severely damaged schools, hospitals, homes, and water systems, leaving hundreds of thousands of civilians vulnerable to worsening humanitarian conditions.
Children are also facing long-term consequences from the conflict, including psychological trauma, displacement, the risk of recruitment by armed groups, abduction, and sexual violence.
Humanitarian organizations have called on all parties involved in the conflict to protect civilians, stop attacks on essential infrastructure, and guarantee safe access for emergency assistance as violence continues across several regions of Sudan.

excerpt: Djibouti City, July 6, 2026 - Former Djiboutian minister and veteran diplomat Hawa Ahmed Youssouf has released a new book offering a rare behind-the-scenes account of more than a decade of peace mediation across Africa, shedding light on the diplomatic efforts that shaped…
title_en: Former Djiboutian Diplomat Chronicles Thirteen Years of African Peace Mediation
excerpt_en: Djibouti City, July 6, 2026 - Former Djiboutian minister and veteran diplomat Hawa Ahmed Youssouf has released a new book offering a rare behind-the-scenes account of more than a decade of peace mediation across Africa, shedding light on the diplomatic efforts that shaped…
body_en:
Djibouti City, July 6, 2026 - Former Djiboutian minister and veteran diplomat Hawa Ahmed Youssouf has released a new book offering a rare behind-the-scenes account of more than a decade of peace mediation across Africa, shedding light on the diplomatic efforts that shaped conflict resolution between 2010 and 2023.
Titled Djiboutian Diplomat at the Heart of African Turmoils (Central African Republic, Madagascar, Comoros, Mali) 2010-2023, the publication recounts her experience in some of the continent's most complex political and security crises, drawing on firsthand involvement in mediation initiatives led under the auspices of the African Union.
Across nearly 300 pages, Hawa Ahmed Youssouf reflects on her diplomatic career, including her appointment in 2010 as the first African woman to serve as a Special Representative of the African Union. The book documents negotiations, peace initiatives, and conflict-resolution efforts carried out in the Central African Republic, Madagascar, the Comoros, and Mali, while providing readers with an insider's perspective on the challenges of crisis diplomacy.
Rather than serving solely as a personal memoir, the publication examines the practical realities of preventive diplomacy and peacebuilding, illustrating how dialogue, negotiation, and compromise are often conducted away from public attention to prevent violence and restore political stability.
The narrative also explores the complex environment in which African mediators operate, including political rivalries, competing international interests, institutional fragility, and the humanitarian consequences of conflict. Through her experiences, the author emphasizes that diplomatic progress often depends on patience, trust-building, persistence, and sustained dialogue among opposing parties.
Alongside her professional journey, Hawa Ahmed Youssouf recounts her personal story, reflecting on her upbringing, educational path, and the challenges she overcame to become one of Djibouti's most prominent diplomats. She pays tribute to the role of her family, particularly her mother, whose encouragement and belief in education helped shape her career.
The publication also highlights the growing contribution of women to diplomacy, mediation, and peacebuilding across Africa, underscoring their increasing presence in leadership and decision-making positions within continental institutions.
For Djibouti, the book represents both a historical record and a recognition of the country's contribution to African diplomacy. By documenting key moments in regional peace efforts, it adds to the continent's diplomatic history while offering valuable insights for researchers, students, policymakers, and future generations interested in conflict resolution and international relations.
Released at a time when Africa continues to face complex security challenges, the work serves as a reminder of the critical role of diplomacy, cooperation, and political dialogue in promoting peace and long-term stability across the continent.

title: Rwanda Praises Pakistan's Role in US-Iran Peace Efforts at Liberation Day Event
excerpt: ISLAMABAD, Pakistan, July 6, 2026 - Rwanda has commended Pakistan for its role in facilitating diplomatic efforts that contributed to a peace agreement between the United States and Iran, describing the initiative as an important contribution to regional and international…
title_en: Rwanda Praises Pakistan's Role in US-Iran Peace Efforts at Liberation Day Event
excerpt_en: ISLAMABAD, Pakistan, July 6, 2026 - Rwanda has commended Pakistan for its role in facilitating diplomatic efforts that contributed to a peace agreement between the United States and Iran, describing the initiative as an important contribution to regional and international…
body_en:
ISLAMABAD, Pakistan, July 6, 2026 - Rwanda has commended Pakistan for its role in facilitating diplomatic efforts that contributed to a peace agreement between the United States and Iran, describing the initiative as an important contribution to regional and international stability.
The remarks were made during celebrations marking Rwanda's 32nd Liberation Day in Islamabad, where Rwanda's Ambassador to Pakistan, Fatou Harerimana, thanked the Pakistani government for supporting dialogue that began in Islamabad and culminated in the signing of a peace agreement in Switzerland following the conflict between the United States and Iran.
The ambassador also highlighted the growing partnership between Rwanda and Pakistan, saying the two countries continue to strengthen cooperation across multiple sectors based on shared interests and mutual respect. She noted Rwanda's progress over the past three decades, attributing the country's transformation to sustained efforts in governance, innovation, and economic development.
Representing the Pakistani government, Minister of State for Law and Justice Barrister Aqeel Malik reaffirmed Pakistan's commitment to expanding bilateral relations with Rwanda. He also said Rwanda's Liberation Day symbolizes the restoration of peace and stability following the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi and acknowledged the country's progress in reconstruction and development.

title_en: Walikale: Four Young Men Allegedly Executed by AFC/M23 Over Suspected Links With Wazalendo
excerpt_en: Walikale, July 6, 2026 - Four young men were reportedly killed on Sunday, July 5, in Ihula, located in the Kisimba area of Walikale territory, North Kivu, after being accused by AFC/M23 fighters of collaborating with Wazalendo self-defense groups. The deaths were confirmed by…
body_en:
Walikale, July 6, 2026 - Four young men were reportedly killed on Sunday, July 5, in Ihula, located in the Kisimba area of Walikale territory, North Kivu, after being accused by AFC/M23 fighters of collaborating with Wazalendo self-defense groups.
The deaths were confirmed by traditional authorities in the Kisimba area, who stated that the victims were allegedly executed before being buried on the same day in Ihula.
According to local sources, AFC/M23 forces have increasingly accused residents in areas under their control of cooperating with either Wazalendo fighters or the Congolese armed forces (FARDC). These accusations have reportedly contributed to growing fear among local communities.
Residents and traditional leaders also report that several civilians arrested in recent months over similar allegations remain missing, leaving families without information about their whereabouts or fate.
In Kisimba and surrounding areas of Walikale territory, where AFC/M23 maintains control, inhabitants describe a deteriorating security environment marked by arrests, alleged abuses, and concerns over possible reprisals.
No official reaction from AFC/M23 authorities regarding the allegations had been reported at the time of publication. The situation remains tense as local communities continue to call for protection and greater attention to civilian safety.

excerpt: KIGALI, Rwanda, July 6, 2026 - Rwandan Senator Evode Uwizeyimana has argued that the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) cannot be effectively neutralized without addressing what he described as its close integration with the Armed Forces of the Democratic…
title_en: Rwandan Senator Says Neutralizing FDLR Depends on FARDC Action
excerpt_en: KIGALI, Rwanda, July 6, 2026 - Rwandan Senator Evode Uwizeyimana has argued that the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) cannot be effectively neutralized without addressing what he described as its close integration with the Armed Forces of the Democratic…
body_en:
KIGALI, Rwanda, July 6, 2026 - Rwandan Senator Evode Uwizeyimana has argued that the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) cannot be effectively neutralized without addressing what he described as its close integration with the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC).
Speaking in an interview, the senator referred to the peace agreement signed in Washington on June 27, 2026, which calls for the dismantling of the FDLR and the eventual lifting of Rwanda's border security measures. He maintained that the FDLR and elements of the Congolese army are so closely linked that separating the two would be extremely difficult.
Uwizeyimana said Rwanda should maintain its current border security measures until the FDLR is effectively dismantled, arguing that removing them before then would expose the country to significant security risks. He added that, in his view, any potential diplomatic or economic consequences of maintaining the measures would be less severe than the security risks associated with lifting them prematurely.
His remarks come as debate continues over the implementation of the Washington peace agreement. Rwandan military officials have previously stated that the country's security measures were introduced in response to cross-border security threats and would be reviewed in line with developments on the ground.
